| Notes | | |
| | Matt Olson's 2025 results fell short of his peak power standards, but remained consistent in other areas. For the fourth year in a row, the 32-year-old played in all 162 games and flirted with another 30/100/100 season. His 2026 projections still forecast elite home run totals and strong RBI production, supported by consistent barrel rates and everyday cleanup duties in Atlanta. Olson's 2025 batting average (.272) was buoyed by a .333 BABIP, so expect regression to around the .250 mark this year. His power floor is among the safest at the position. Olson profiles as a reliable early-round source of HR and RBI, particularly valuable in formats that de-emphasize average. Kelly Kirby - FantasyPros | |

item.title: [MLB.com] Which Blue Jays could be up for award hardware?
item.dc:creator: Keegan Matheson
item.description: TORONTO -- The long wait is almost over for the Blue Jays, who have been stuck waiting for the offseason to roll around for over a month now. On this day last year, the Blue Jays won Game 5 of the World Series in Los Angeles, sending the series back to Toronto with a 3-2 lead over the Dodgers. The 365 days since then haven’t been very kind to Canada’s team. It’s time to work on turning this back around, though, and that finally gets rolling soon: Key November dates First day after World Series:
item.content:encoded:
TORONTO -- The long wait is almost over for the Blue Jays, who have been stuck waiting for the offseason to roll around for over a month now.
On this day last year, the Blue Jays won Game 5 of the World Series in Los Angeles, sending the series back to Toronto with a 3-2 lead over the Dodgers. The 365 days since then haven’t been very kind to Canada’s team.
It’s time to work on turning this back around, though, and that finally gets rolling soon:
Key November dates
First day after World Series: Players become free agents; players may be traded between clubs
Five days after World Series (5 p.m. ET): Deadline for teams to make a qualifying offer to players; players can begin signing with any club
Nov. 10-12: General Managers Meetings in Las Vegas
Nov. 17 (4 p.m. ET): Deadline for players to accept a qualifying offer
Nov. 20: Tender deadline
Major League Baseball’s award season will also feature some Blue Jays content, especially with their five finalists for the AL Gold Glove Awards. Here’s a look at how the awards could break down and which Blue Jays will be involved.
Award watch: Gold Gloves
The Gold Glove Awards will be announced on Sunday on ESPN, with the broadcast beginning at 8:30 p.m. ET.
1B Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
Yes, this one will require you to remember, just for a moment, that the Gold Glove Award is strictly a defensive award. It’s easy to lose this in the mess of a season Guerrero just went through, but his defense was excellent, and if you can look at that in a silo, you’ll see one of his best seasons as a big leaguer. Guerrero’s fielding run value of +6 was the third best among first basemen in the American League, and the eye test backed that up with both fundamental plays and some highlight-reel scoops and dives. He’ll be up against Vinnie Pasquantino of the Royals and Christian Walker of the Astros.
SS Andrés Giménez
It felt like Giménez got better as the year went on, finally settling in as the club’s shortstop after spending most of his big league career at second. Giménez already has three Gold Glove Awards (2022, ‘23, ‘24) from his time with the Guardians, and his +16 fielding run value ranks him second in the AL behind only Bobby Witt Jr. of the Royals. Along with Witt, Taylor Walls of the Rays rounds out the finalists.
RF Nathan Lukes
It’s great to see Lukes get this recognition as a finalist. His defense is criminally underrated, which kept showing up in games when opponents would try to run on Lukes. He’s up against Wilyer Abreu of the Red Sox and Cam Smith of the Astros.
C Brandon Valenzuela
If Valenzuela had started 115 games behind the plate, he might just run away with this award. He and Alejandro Kirk tied for third in the AL at +11 fielding run value, and Valenzuela did that with just 68 starts behind the plate. With his blocking, framing and incredible throwing arm, there might be a couple of these in Valenzuela’s future. He’s up against Dillon Dingler of the Tigers and Austin Wells of the Yankees.
SP José Soriano
Pitchers are always the most difficult race to measure, but Soriano’s reputation as a good fielder and strong athlete have been recognized here. He’ll be up against Tanner Bibee of the Guardians and Jacob deGrom of the Rangers.
Award watch: Everything else
It’s possible that Kazuma Okamoto gets some outside consideration for the AL Rookie of the Year Award after launching 33 home runs in his first MLB season, but his age (30) coming over from Japan adds an interesting wrinkle when compared to players in their early 20s who came up through the Minor Leagues.
Dylan Cease’s case for the Cy Young Award feels like the Blue Jays’ best shot to rank in the top three on a ballot, though. For much of the season, Cease and New York’s Cam Schlittler were in a dead heat, but Schlittler appears to have pulled away down the stretch while Cease’s case faded and he eventually landed on the IL. Regardless, Cease’s season is worth celebrating.
In the first year of his seven-year, $210 million deal, Cease put up a 2.40 ERA with 239 strikeouts over 169 innings, which included some absolutely dominant stretches through the middle of the summer. He’s been everything the Blue Jays could have hoped for and more.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Ex-Tigers Ace Tarik Skubal Crosses One Potential Suitor Off His List

item.description: Because they weren't able to come to an agreement with ace pitcher Tarik Skubal before the 2026 MLB Trade Deadline, the Detroit Tigers shipped him to the defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers in return for a trio of prospects. Skubal can become an unrestricted free agent af
item.content:encoded:
Because they weren't able to come to an agreement with ace pitcher Tarik Skubal before the 2026 MLB Trade Deadline, the Detroit Tigers shipped him to the defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers in return for a trio of prospects.
Skubal and the Dodgers were swept out of the National League Championship Series by the Milwaukee Brewers, ending any dreams of becoming the first team in over 25 years to win three straight World Series titles.
Skubal can become an unrestricted free agent after the conclusion of the World Series, and he's in line to land a record-breaking new contract. But which team will be the one to step up to the plate and hand him a giant deal?
According to the latest reports, at least one major contender to land Skubal can take their name off his list of potential destinations.
Ex-Detroit Tigers Ace Tarik Skubal Crosses One Potential Suitor Off His List
According to former Toronto Blue Jays outfielder Kevin Pillar, Skubal won't be coming to the Jays.
When asked about the chances of Toronto extending an offer/making a play to land Skubal, Pillar said he didn't believe that it will happen.
"I don't," Pillar said. "They got their ace, they got Dylan Cease and as much as you want to build your team around having this elite starting pitching, I think the Blue Jays have good starting pitching. You can never have enough starting pitching."
"I think the Blue Jays learned this year that they need to distribute that money over position groups as opposed to going out to sign Skubal."
The Blue Jays, who came within a single victory of winning the World Series last fall, failed to defend their American League Championship of 2025 when they failed to make the playoffs this year.
Tarik Skubal Left The Door Open To Returning To The Tigers
Not long after being acquired by the Dodgers, Skubal left the door open to potentially returning to the Tigers at some point.
"I would love to play my whole career in Detroit. I would love to," Skubal explained in an interview with Pardon My Take. "And hopefully those negotiations can pick back up in November once the playoffs are done. We'll see where that goes. Hopefully they're involved with everything. I would love to return."
Meanwhile, he also lamented the fact that the Tigers weren't able to live up to their expectations of competing for the World Series.
"This wasn't the way the season was supposed to go. Going into the offseason, [with] the people that we acquired through free agency and who we signed, I'm like, 'This is the World Series team,'" Skubal said. "This is the team that I'm gonna go and win a World Series and beat anybody. It doesn't matter what's going on."
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Ex-Tigers Ace Tarik Skubal Crosses One Potential Suitor Off His List appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Cam Schlittler Named AL Outstanding Pitcher by His Fellow MLB Players
item.dc:creator: Chris Trant
item.description: The New York Yankees put together a strong regular season during the 2026 MLB season, finishing 93-68 and earning the top American League Wild Card spot before sweeping the Boston Red Sox in the opening round of the postseason. However, their postseason run came to a screeching halt in the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays. The Yankees were swept by the Rays, who would eventually go on to win the American League Pennant. While New York's season ended in disappointment, one of the biggest positives
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees put together a strong regular season during the 2026 MLB season, finishing 93-68 and earning the top American League Wild Card spot before sweeping the Boston Red Sox in the opening round of the postseason.
However, their postseason run came to a screeching halt in the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays. The Yankees were swept by the Rays, who would eventually go on to win the American League Pennant. While New York's season ended in disappointment, one of the biggest positives from the year was the emergence of right-hander Cam Schlittler in his second MLB season.
Schlittler started 33 games for the Yankees this season, going 14-6 and posting an American League-leading 1.95 ERA, with 239 strikeouts and a 0.92 WHIP over 193.2 innings. Schlittler was one of the most dominant pitchers in the American League this season and is a heavy favorite to win the AL Cy Young Award for 2026.
While Schlittler will have to wait until Nov. 11 for the Cy Young voting results, the Yankees announced on Wednesday that the right-hander was named the 2026 Players Choice Awards AL Outstanding Pitcher.
Presented by the MLB Players Association, the award is voted on by active players across the league. Schlittler was among three finalists, including Dylan Cease of the Toronto Blue Jays and Sonny Gray of the Boston Red Sox.
After showing promise as a rookie in 2025, the 25-year-old made a significant leap in his second year and earned his first career All-Star selection.
Schlittler also carried his regular season success into the postseason, where he pitched 6⅓ scoreless innings, striking out 10 in Game 1 of the Wild Card series against the Red Sox.
With the Players Choice Award now added to his résumé, Schlittler has quickly become one of the most accomplished young pitchers in baseball.
Greatest Yankees of All-Time

item.content:encoded:
In perhaps a precursor to the American League Cy Young Award voting, Toronto Blue Jays pitcher Dylan Cease was not named as the Most Outstanding American League Pitcher of the Year, falling in the voting to Cam Schlittler of the New York Yankees.
The awards are voted on by the MLB Players Association.
Regardless of result, it was a great first season in Toronto for Cease, who signed a seven-year, $210 million deal last offseason.
The right-hander made 29 starts around two short injured list stints, going 11-6 with a 2.40 ERA. The Blue Jays had the fewest runs scored and fewest home runs in baseball this season, so Cease and the pitching staff were forced to carry the offense. And Cease certainly did his part.
He struck out 239 batters in just 169.0 innings, marking his sixth straight season of 200 strikeouts or more. He also led the American League in hits/9, strikeouts/9, and home runs/9.
An eight-year veteran of the Chicago White Sox, San Diego Padres and Blue Jays, he's 76-64 in his career with a 3.67 ERA.
He made the All-Star Game for the first time this season, earning the start for the American League, which was managed by Jays' skipper John Schneider.
He ended the year on the IL with shoulder inflammation but is expected to be healthy for spring training.
As for Cam Schlittler
The 25-year-old Massachusetts native made his major league debut in 2025 and has taken the league by storm ever since. Armed with a fastball in the upper-90s, he went 14-6 with a minuscule 1.95 ERA this season, also striking out 239 batters. In 193.2 innings, he had a WHIP of just 0.92. He was a major reason why the Yankees won the American League East and advanced to the American League Division Series, where they were beaten by the Tampa Bay Rays.
Elsewhere for the Blue Jays...
The Milwaukee Brewers currently lead the Rays 3-1 in the World Series with Game 5 set to come on Wednesday night.
If the Rays win, the series will shift back to Milwaukee for Game 6 on Friday, but if the Rays lose, the season is over.
Once the season ends, the pending free agents for the Blue Jays will officially exit the 40-man roster. The Blue Jays will then have five days to get their 40-man roster in compliance and free agency will begin.
However, it's unclear how active free agency will be in November as a result of the looming MLB lockout.

item.content:encoded:
The 2025 season provided ideal outcomes for fantasy managers who invested in elite starting pitchers. That season, Tarik Skubal, Paul Skenes, Garrett Crochet and Zack Wheeler were the top four pitchers drafted. Per our Fantasy Player Rater, Skubal ($35.5), Crochet ($32.8) and Skenes ($30.8) finished 1-2-3 among starting pitchers in all roto formats. Wheeler finished 14th ($22.6) despite his season being cut short. As is the case every single year, to varying degrees, there were mid-round arms who produced elite roto seasons (Bryan Woo, Hunter Brown, Max Fried), as well starters such as Nathan Eovaldi, Matthew Boyd, and Trevor Rogers who provided hefty profit a as late-round picks and free agent acquisitions.
As is also the case every season, there were early-round landmines. Cole Ragans, Blake Snell, and Corbin Burnes all missed at least two-thirds of the season due to injuries. Logan Gilbert investors certainly weren’t thrilled about his abbreviated season with only six wins. Nevertheless, dream seasons from the Crème de la crème instilled an illusion of tranquility at the top of the SP pool for 2026 drafts despite the position’s inherent risks and volatile history.
The calm ominously turned to storm on Opening Day. Paul Skenes couldn’t get out of the first inning against the Mets, allowing five earned runs, as droves of social media melodramatics scolded us: “…and that’s why you never draft pitchers early!” Skenes (174 IP – 200 K – 10 W – 3.82 – 1.12) inevitably lost “fantasy god” status as his price dropped a couple of rounds for 2027 drafts. Skubal was a top 10 pitcher with elite ratios, but did not have his usual season of dominance due to missing 5-6 starts. Crochet was an injury landmine and one of many early-round busts.
There were some wins in the second tier (Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Chris Sale) as well as disappointments (Bryan Woo, Hunter Brown, Ragans again), but what may be most memorable about last season’s starting pitcher pool was that leagues were won without having to invest in early starting pitchers at all. Of course, that only happened to managers who side-stepped the early-round hitter landmines like Aaron Judge, Ronald Acuña Jr., Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Francisco Lindor and Cal Raleigh. The two top producers – Jacob Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler – were post-100 ADP picks. Of the 19 starters who earned $14 or more in 12-team leagues, 13 had an ADP of 100+, including six with an ADP of 250 or greater.

A quick review of this group shouldn’t elicit much bewilderment besides maybe Nick Martinez. Most of the other top performers with a post-100 ADP were former prospects with breakout and profit potential. Let’s run through each set of five rounds by 2026 NFBC Online Championship (OC) 12-team ADP to review results in relation to draft price. Expect some takeaways for 2027 drafts along the way. Pitchers who were traded are listed with the team they were on in March.
| Player | Team | ADP | SP Rank | $ Earned |
|---|---|---|---|---|

| Tarik Skubal | DET | 6.9 | 8 | $22.8 |
| Paul Skenes | PIT | 9.8 | 30 | $9.9 |
| Garrett Crochet | BOS | 12.0 | 113 | -$7.7 |

SP Rank, $ Earned: FanGraphs Fantasy Player Rater
These are the pitchers with ADPs in the first five rounds of OCs. Ohtani could technically be excluded since he was mostly used as a hitter in NFBC formats last season. He did earn nearly $14, producing sparkling ratios (1.79 ERA, 0.95 WHIP) with 95 strikeouts in 85.2 innings (14 starts). Ohtani should pitch again next season, but will be a top-three consensus fantasy pick regardless. No matter where he signs, Skubal will be the first or second SP off draft boards, along with Misiorowski. Sale, Yamamoto and Cristopher Sánchez will likely live in the Round 2 range. Sale was the SP3 in 2024, SP20 in 2025 and SP4 in 2026. Yamamoto was the SP7 and SP3 in his first two full Major League seasons. Sánchez has posted consecutive seasons of 200+ innings and a sub-3.00 ERA. Hunter Brown will be a polarizing pick in the Rounds 4-7 range coming off a 20-start season where he produced a strong 3.19 ERA, but saw his WHIP and walk rate balloon from the previous season — from 1.03 and 7.8% to 1.27 and 12.2%.
A fantasy bust in 2026, Freddy Peralta is quickly surging back up confidence meters and draft boards with his dominant playoff performances. Bryan Woo and Logan Gilbert will be slightly discounted coming off disappointing seasons, but T-Mobile Park in Seattle remains advantageous to starting pitchers (30-of-30 in MLB Park Factor for hits in 2026) and bounce-backs wouldn’t be shocking, assuming good health. Ragans underwent UCL repair surgery in July and has a 10-12 month return timetable, so he’s off our radars for the forseeable future. Jacob deGrom was slightly more human in his age-38 season, posting a career-worst 4.20 ERA, albeit with a 3.11 FIP, 3.14 xFIP and 3.15 SIERA.
Fried’s UCL is “in a good place” according to NY Daily News writer, Gary Phillips. Logan Webb is no longer the position’s Iron Man and could fall out of the top 100 ADP, though he will always have supporters. A healthy Webb could provide profit at a reasonable cost.

| Cam Schlittler | NYY | 119.2 | 2 | $37.1 |
SP Rank, $ Earned: FanGraphs Fantasy Player Rater
The 61-120 ADP range was quite the mixed bag.
Dylan Cease and Jesús Luzardo were studs and will be drafted in the top 50 in most formats.
Wheeler recovered thoroughly from his thoracic outlet procedure and produced yet another $20+ season: 162 IP (28 starts) – 193 K – 14 W – 3.00 – 1.05. He has been the best pitcher in the Majors since 2021, leading in wins (79), ERA (2.92) and second in strikeouts (1,234) behind Cease’s 1,345.
Chase Burns will be highly coveted after his masterful performance over his first full season (154.1 IP – 185 K – 15 W – 2.86 – 1.17) and will be drafted among the top 12 to 15 starters. Nolan McLean will be slightly cheaper than Burns after his first full and successful season in the Majors. Cases made against either this offseason will start with concerns about their lack of elite control and potential WHIP damage at Tier 2 SP prices. Eury Pérez is in this boat as well after posting a 10.3% walk rate and a 1.21 WHIP, though don’t expect to pay anything but a premium for the coveted fireballer who will turn 24 in April.
Joe Ryan should be a solid pick among the top 100 as well. Though he may never have that 180+ IP dream season where good health and all the cards align, Ryan has been a dependable fantasy stud, posting a K-BB% over 20% for four straight seasons and has made between 23 and 30 starts over his first five full seasons.
There were quite a few negative value guys in this range, which was quite shocking for some: George Kirby, Kyle Bradish, Framber Valdez, Kevin Gausman and Emmet Sheehan. Kirby is quickly becoming persona non grata in the fantasy community, posting a painful 1.40 WHIP last season and two straight years with a 4.00+ ERA. Bradish’s WHIP (1.42) was even worse than Kirby’s as he did most of his damage after the All-Star break, posting a 5.29 ERA and a .398 wOBA in those final 10 starts before getting shelved due to lower abdominal pain and being diagnosed with a sports hernia. Gausman compiled 30+ starts for a sixth consecutive season. Despite nearly all of his rate stats and underlying metrics matching last season’s, Gausman posted a 4.51 ERA, with an xFIP and SIERA over a full run lower. I’ll remind myself of how solid everything looked under the hood for Gausman and would consider targeting him again in 2027 drafts. Sheehan isn’t going to fly under the radar this draft season despite last year’s poor results. The key here, of course, is Sheehan having a rotation spot. He dominated in his time down in Triple-A and fired three gems for the Dodgers in September (0.53 ERA, 24:3 K:BB in 17 innings/3 starts).

|---|---|---|---|---|

SP Rank, $ Earned: FanGraphs Fantasy Player Rater
The 120-180 ADP range was Landmine Central — pitchers like Castillo, Imai, and Chandler decimated our ratios. There were likely some folks who were duped for another round of category destruction when Castillo joined the White Sox. Castillo’s 5.85 ERA was third-worst among the 94 pitchers who threw at least 130 innings. The only ones worse were Kyle Freeland (6.65) and Jeffrey Springs (6.18). At least both of them had bad home parks as an excuse.
Rasmussen and Gray sported matching 2.72 ERAs and finished as top 12 starters. Both will be highly coveted by drafters and I’m sure that the Rasmussen helium will take soar him into the third round of 12-teamers, especially with the glow of playoff glory. Gray dazzled with a below-average strikeout rate of 21.8%, which was 6-7% lower than his two previous seasons in St. Louis. Because of some peripheral drop-offs and his age (36), don’t be surprised to see Gray fall into some offseason bust articles.
Imanaga had three massive disaster starts in the second half of May, but his overall production was strong and his control is on the border of elite. He posted a 5.2% walk rate and a 24.6% strikeout rate and owns a 19.4% K-BB% over three Major League seasons. He’s a free agent who the Cubs would love to re-sign, though we should expect the Padres to show strong interest. I’m definitely interested in Imanaga next season.
Robbie Ray is also a free agent who should generate offseason interest. He will certainly experience a price dip from the 100s to the 200s after a visit from the control boogie man (12% BB) last season.
Gavin Williams led the AL in strikeouts, fueled by an impressive 15% swinging-strike rate. More importantly, he reduced a near-12% walk rate down to below nine percent last season. Williams won’t be cheap in drafts, and rightfully so.

| Ryan Weathers | NYY | 237.1 | 67 | $1.2 |
SP Rank, $ Earned: FanGraphs Fantasy Player Rater
There were some stretches of fantasy usefulness from several in this tier, but no big payoffs. Ryan Weathers’ first season in the AL was a roller coaster ride, but mostly positive. He finished the season with a 3.60 ERA aligned with peripherals (3.50 SIERA, 3.44 xFIP), a 1.22 WHIP, and a 18.5% K-BB%. His roto value was weighed down by just five victories. Carlos Rodón was a properly discounted stash who was activated on May 10 and pitched nine starts before elbow inflammation reappeared and he missed two months of the summer. The end-of-season line was good (2.67 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 26.8% K in 16 starts). His 11.2% walk rate wasn’t and it was his first season over 10% in the post-Covid era. An air of trepidation will likely always remain for Rodón because of his elbow, which may result in a 2027 discount, with profitability a likely outcome if his UCL stays intact.
Jack Flaherty and Zac Gallen are falling semi-stars who were unmitigated disasters last season. Gallen finished with a 3-9 record and a 6.07 ERA in 105.1 innings. Flaherty threw just 88.1 innings and had a 4.48 ERA with his typical high strikeout rate (26%). Flaherty and Gallen are both free agents. They’ll be more appealing to real-life teams than to fantasy managers.
Tanner Bibee makes 30 starts a season, but is essentially just a thrower now. He has posted an ERA over 4.00 for a second straight season and has seen his strikeout rate reduced in three consecutive seasons — from 26.3% to 21.3% to 19%. Bibee has three years left on his 5yr, $45M deal.
Trey Yesavage was certainly trending toward Miz and Schlittler range this winter and early spring, earning a minimum pick of 113 in Online Championships. Yesavage ADP helium was quickly popped a week before Opening Day because of right shoulder impingement. In the Too Early Meatball draft in August, Yesavage was drafted in the 15th round, and this is a 15-team format. It would hard to imagine Yesavage not rising up boards back into the top 150 overall. He has a spot in the Jays rotation so all he needs know is to stay healthy.

SP Rank, $ Earned: FanGraphs Fantasy Player Rater
A long list of names, so we’ll just touch on a few of them. Among the studs who provided tremendous profit were Cade Cavalli, Reid Detmers, Nick Martinez, Payton Tolle, and the impenetrable Eduardo Rodriguez, who pulled off 17 wins with a 2.89 ERA despite a much higher xFIP (4.44) and SIERA (4.62) and the lowest BABIP (.274 of his career). I don’t usually mess with the peripheral gods and will stubbornly skip over him in early drafts. Cade Cavalli had an epic run after the All-Star break, posting a 90:16 K:BB and a 1.90 ERA over his final 12 starts. Reid Detmers was having a decent season, but really began to shine when the Angels fired pitching coach Mike Maddux. Over those final 8 starts, Detmers posted a 4-0 record with a 1.62 ERA and an impressive 55:5 K:BB. Angels fans are hoping that the new regime under new owner Stan Kroenke will bring the organization from the basement to at least the living room. Interim GM John Mozeliak will stay in the role for now and help the Angels find a permanent GM and a new manager, since Kurt Suzuki is one-and-done.
A $1.20 earning shouldn’t detract from the admiration that Clay Holmes should receive after Round 15 in 12-teamers. He produced a respectable 3.29 ERA, but his low value was impacted by a low strikeout rate (18.6%), six wins, and time spent on the IL, which led to just 18 starts on the season. Michael Wacha was stellar yet again, earning $10 in 12-team NFBC roto leagues as the SP29. Taj Bradley, Troy Melton, Ian Seymour, Justin Wrobleski, and Michael Soroka all had some strong stretches of production that helped fantasy managers, especially those who got out of the Wrobleski business before that ship began to sank. Seymour and Melton are already earning some early 2027 draft love, getting scooped up among the top 50 starters in the 150-175 ADP range — a price that is likely to surge as we move through the heart of draft season.
Finally, a shout out to FAAB stud Sean Burke who broke out in a big way. He produced a 3.34 ERA, a 1.20 WHIP and punched out 185 batters over 172.1 innings. Burke had a scorching-hot nine-start run from June 18 through August 11 where he rocked a 1.60 ERA and struck out 79, with just 11 walks over 62 innings. He had some rough starts, but was still worth every free agent penny. Based on some of the prices (2-5% of budget), it almost felt like pennies were what were being spent.
It’s always a good idea to dig into player stats not long after the season has ended. It helps avoid building biases that may fester, resonate, and solidify within our draft tendencies for the coming draft season. When we wait too long into the winter to review individual player profiles, we increase the likelihood of outside influences manipulating our valuations of players — whether it’s articles that do a good job of convincing a player is a boon or a bust, social media bandwaggoning, or ADP data itself. We don’t have to decide between Ashcraft and McLean now, but if we’re equipped with the details of their stats, underlying metrics, velocity trends, pitch mix changes, Stuff, and healthy history, we can limit emotion and bias from our decision-making and make optimal, objective decisions during the heart of draft season.
Vlad writes for RotoGraphs and is the head of fantasy baseball content at FTN Fantasy. He is a Tout Wars Expert League champ, member of the CDM Fantasy Sports Hall of Fame and has been nominated for FSWA writing awards six times. Vlad has been playing fantasy baseball since 1995, winning 42 NFBC leagues since 2012 and ranking in the top percentile in NFBC’s Online Championship contest (33% win rate, 52% cash rate; 64 leagues). Much to the chagrin of his colleagues and most baseball aficionados, Vlad is a lifelong Dodgers fan who claims his first gut call at age 9 was Kirk Gibson’s 1988 World Series home run. You can follow him on X and BlueSky @RotoGut.

item.dc:creator: Eric Samulski

item.content:encoded:
The World Series is about to begin, and we’re being treated to a doozy of a series between the Brewers and the Rays. However, for the 28 other teams, they are turning their attention to 2027, so we’ll join them in that for a bit with some starting pitcher rankings for next season.
This is now my fourth year publishing my starting pitcher rankings and my second year doing it this early. In many ways, I like doing a first pass at rankings this year. At this point, it’s hard to overthink. Most players aren’t playing games or posting videos of new pitches, so there is nothing to get geeked about. Instead, these rankings are more “gut feel” rankings based on how I feel about all of these pitchers at the end of the season. While I tried not to get too in the weeds about stats, I did look back at the general profile that allowed a pitcher to finish among the top 30 overall starters in recent years, and tried to prioritize pitchers who fit that profile, which mostly meant elevating pitchers who get swings and misses, and penalizing pitchers who don’t seem like a good bet for a full season of innings.
As always, the pitchers are split into tiers based on their skillset or what they’ll provide your fantasy team. The tiers themselves are more important than the rankings inside the tiers, so I wouldn’t split hairs over a few spots in the rankings. I’ve also ranked these pitchers as if I’m doing a 12-team league, so safe but boring low-end starters take a hit in value, etc. I won’t have really long write-ups here, but I’ll be back with updated rankings after the new year, where we can get a little more into the nitty-gritty of the rankings.
OK? Ok, so let’s get started.
2027 Fantasy Baseball Starting Pitcher Rankings
| Rank | Player | Team | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| Aces | | | | |
| 1 | Jacob Misiorowski | MIL | No | Aces |
| 2 | Tarik Skubal | Free Agent | No | Aces |
| 3 | Cam Schlittler | NYY | No | Aces |
| 4 | Cristopher Sánchez | PHI | No | Aces |
| 5 | Yoshinobu Yamamoto | LAD | No | Aces |
There’s not much to discuss about these aces. All five posted a K-BB% of at least 21%, and four of them carried a Stuff+ of 113 or higher. They seem like the clear top five starters in baseball, if they can remain healthy.
| Fringe Young Aces | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 6 | Chase Burns | CIN | No | Young power arms |
| 7 | Payton Tolle | BOS | No | Young power arms |
| 8 | Logan Gilbert | SEA | No | Strikeout guys |
| 9 | Paul Skenes | PIT | No - Maybe? | Young power arms |
There’s an argument to be made for all of these guys being aces. Obviously, Paul Skenes is the key name because he was an ace coming into last season and then posted a
3.82 ERA with a 3.34 SIERA. His Stuff+ also fell from 110 in 2025 to 99 this past season, and he didn’t look fully healthy. Still, he’s one year removed from a 1.97 ERA over 187 IP and was the best young arm in baseball. It’s hard to completely ignore 2024 and 2025. All four of these guys finished with a K-BB% between 20% and 22%, and all are power-first pitchers. Chase Burns threw 154.1 IP with a 2.86 ERA, 3.46 SIERA, 14.4% SwStr%, and 112 Stuff+, and I think that innings number will rise, which will give him even more value. Payton Tolle’s first full season was 148.2 IP with a 3.03 ERA, 21.7% K-BB, and 115 Stuff+. Like Burns, I also expect his innings to rise and his value to tick up.
| Aces With Injury Risk | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 10 | Chris Sale | ATL | No (Previous risk) | Elite vets, health risk |
| 11 | Garrett Crochet | BOS | Yes | Elite vets, health risk |
| 12 | Jacob deGrom | TEX | No (Previous risk) | Elite vets, health risk |
| 13 | Zack Wheeler | PHI | Yes | Elite vets, health risk |
| 14 | Bryan Woo | SEA | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 15 | Jesús Luzardo | PHI | No | Elite vets, health risk |
| 16 | Dylan Cease | TOR | Yes | Elite vets, health risk |
If you wanted to take any of these starters over the guys in the tier above, that wouldn’t be crazy. They’re not down in this tier because they’re worse pitchers; they’re in this tier because they carry more injury risk than the pitchers in the tier above, and injury risk with your ace is a serious gamble. Chris Sale and Jacob deGrom have been healthy the last two years, but have a lengthy injury history, while Garrett Crochet missed essentially the entire year with an injury, and Dylan Cease saw his velocity plummet at the end of the season and then ended the year on the IL with a shoulder injury. You draft this group for ace outcomes at a price that already reflects the innings risk.
| Ace Upside - Limited Track Record | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 17 | Drew Rasmussen | TBR | No (Previous Risk) | WHIP guys |
| 18 | Cade Cavalli | WSN | Coming off injury | Rising arms, unproven |
| 19 | Braxton Ashcraft | PIT | No | Rising arms, unproven |
| 20 | Logan Henderson | MIL | Coming off injury | Rising arms, unproven |
| 21 | Gavin Williams | CLE | No | Rising arms, unproven |
Almost everyone here has one strong season to point to, which is why the tier name fits. Of course, Drew Rasmussen has more than one good season, but he also has had three elbow surgeries and has only pitched over 150 innings once in his MLB career. That prevents me from drafting him where I think his talent should have him because he carries so much extra risk. Cade Cavalli and Logan Henderson also have injury track records that make me a little bit concerned about their durability, and Cavalli’s breakout 2026 season was so closely tied to a velocity increase that I’m just not sure if I want to fully ignore the first three months of the season for him, which were pretty inconsistent. This feels like a fair hedge on the bets for Cavalli. Gavin Williams arguably has the best skills of the group (2.95 SIERA, 25.1% K-BB, 15% SwStr%), but he also had a 3.76 ERA because he is prone to losing his command for an inning in basically every outing.
| High-End SP2 Without Elite K% | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 22 | Parker Messick | CLE | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 23 | Max Fried | NYY | Yes | Weak contact and durability |
| 24 | Griffin Jax | TBR | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 25 | Hunter Brown | HOU | Yes | Weak contact and durability |
These four are valuable because of ERA and WHIP, not big strikeout totals. Parker Messick had moments where he looked like a fantasy ace, but he has just a 97 Stuff+ and his strikeout rate is not the same as the guys in the tier above. Max Fried had another solid season, but his fantasy finishes over the last four years have been super inconsistent because he seems to always miss time with an injury. Hunter Brown was clearly hurt and not pitching well this season, but his strikeout numbers also fell off a cliff in the second half of last season, so I’m not sure we can really rely on him for strikeouts. Griffin Jax is an interesting bet because he only moved into the rotation in the middle of the season, but he had 103.1 innings as a starter and registered a 3.14 ERA, 18.8% K-BB, and 13.6% SwStr%. That’s pretty damn good.
| There’s an Ace in There Somewhere | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 26 | Joe Ryan | MIN | Yes | Strikeout guys |
| 27 | Jared Jones | PIT | Yes | Rising arms, unproven |
| 28 | Reid Detmers | LAA | No | Rising arms, unproven |
| 29 | Blake Snell | LAD | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 30 | Shohei Ohtani | LAD | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 31 | Carlos Rodón | NYY | Yes | Power arms, command concern |
| 32 | Nolan McLean | NYM | No | Young power arms |
| 33 | Eury Pérez | MIA | No | Power arms, command concern |
| 34 | Emmet Sheehan | LAD | No | Rising arms, unproven |
This tier is a bet on ceiling, and the group has the skills to justify it, but not the track record of consistent production. Obviously, Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani, and Carlos Rodon are all in here because of injury concerns that prevent me from giving them enough innings to have them qualify as an ace. Reid Detmers finally had his breakout year in 185.0 innings with a 3.36 ERA and 22.0% K-BB, and Jared Jones shook the rust after his return from injury and pitched 101.2 innings with a 3.28 SIERA and 22.2% K-BB. He really came on at the end of the season. We also still see enough strikeout upside and raw, natural ability from Nolan McLean, Eury Perez, and Emmet Sheehan to have them here. I do worry that McLean had just a 9.6% swinging strike rate, and there may not be as much strikeout upside as people want to believe. This is the range that Misiorowski and Schlittler were going last year, and somebody in here is going to make that jump.
| No Longer Aces, But Safe Floor | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 35 | Gerrit Cole | NYY | No | Strikeout guys |
| 36 | Sonny Gray | BOS | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 37 | Shota Imanaga | Free Agent | No | WHIP guys |
| 38 | Logan Webb | SFG | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 39 | Freddy Peralta | Free Agent | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 40 | Sandy Alcantara | MIA | No | Weak contact and durability |
The pitchers here have a long record of quality, and the case for them is volume and ratios. Sandy Alcantara is probably the weakest of the bunch, but he threw 211 innings this season, and we’re back to getting that bulk production from him; a 4.24 SIERA is just not ideal. Freddy Peralta has turned his season around with the Rays, and we’ve seen him be a good starting pitcher for too long to not assume he can continue to pitch well in 2027.
| Fun Upside With Volatility | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 41 | Ian Seymour | TBR | No | Strikeout guys |
| 42 | Andrew Painter | PHI | No | Strikeout guys |
| 43 | Christian Scott | NYM | No | Power arms, command concern |
| 44 | Kade Anderson | SEA | No | Top prospects, clear 2027 job |
| 45 | Kaima Taira | Intl (NPB) | No | International, unproven |
| 46 | Walbert Ureña | LAA | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
The appeal here is strikeout ability, and the risk is large, which is why they’re all down in this range. Ian Seymour flashed the best MLB skills in the tier. In 77 innings as a starter this season, he posted a 2.84 SIERA, 26.7% K-BB, and 14.4% SwStr%. I know the 4.44 ERA wasn’t tremendous, but I believe in the underlying skill set here. Andrew Painter made some key pitch mix changes in the second half of the season that I really like, but, much like Cavalli, his ability to hold velocity will be crucial. Walbert Ureña is confusing. He throws hard and has a nasty changeup plus a sweeper that flashed the ability to miss bats this season. You watch him pitch, and you see a potential stud. But his four-seamer is pretty average, and his 4.14 SIERA and 12.3% K-BB% say he got lucky this season.
The two biggest wild cards here are Kade Anderson and Kaima Taira. Anderson was the top pitching prospect in baseball, but he relies on command and movement over velocity and raw stuff, so it remains to be seen how that translates at the big league level. Taira is almost certain to come over from Japan this offseason after pitching to a 1.36 ERA and 0.97 WHIP with 134 K and 44 BB over 139 IP in NPB this year. We’ve heard he touches 100 mph, has an eight-pitch mix, and could be the best pitching free agent this offseason, other than Skubal.
| Boring But It Can Work | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 47 | Kevin Gausman | Free Agent | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 48 | Aaron Nola | PHI | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 49 | George Kirby | SEA | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
All of these guys had pretty gross ERAs but underlying metrics that say they pitched better than the results. We just have to decide if we believe that or not. Aaron Nola made some pitch mix changes in the second half (limiting elevated fastballs) that helped him to produce better results, but George Kirby simply never got it going this year. The draft case for each of these guys is innings, a discounted price based on ERA over SIERA, and a decent chance of a bounce-back, with Kevin Gausman the safest of the three, depending on where he signs.
| Hurt But Should Be Healthy Opening Day | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 50 | Nathan Eovaldi | Free Agent | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 51 | Shane McClanahan | TBR | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 52 | Max Meyer | MIA | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 53 | Ryan Weathers | NYY | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 54 | Ryan Pepiot | TBR | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 55 | Pablo López | MIN | Yes | Ace upside, coming off injury |
| 56 | Nick Pivetta | SDP | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 57 | Corbin Burnes | ARI | Yes | Ace upside, coming off injury |
| 58 | Tyler Glasnow | LAD | Yes | Ace upside, coming off injury |
This is another tier of injuries. These guys ended the season hurt or were hurt for basically the entire year. However, all of them seem likely to begin the year healthy and on the mound for their respective teams. You’re drafting them if the injury discount leaves a bigger gap than the missed time justifies.
| Is There a Next Step? | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 59 | Jackson Jobe | DET | Yes | Strikeout guys |
| 60 | Didier Fuentes | ATL | No | Strikeout guys |
| 61 | Trey Yesavage | TOR | Yes | Power arms, command concern |
| 62 | Roki Sasaki | LAD | No | Young power arms |
| 63 | Taj Bradley | MIN | No | Power arms, command concern |
| 64 | Sean Burke | CHW | No | Strikeout guys |
| 65 | Nick Lodolo | CIN | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 66 | River Ryan | DET | Yes | Top prospects, clear 2027 job |
These pitchers have flashed the physical tools, but the consistent results are not there yet. Roki Sasaki, Taj Bradley, and Sean Burke all had stretches in 2026 where they showed clear improvement from 2025. But those stretches didn’t last. Can we count of them in 2027? Trey Yesavage and Jackson Jobe both spent most of the year recovering from injury, but they are top pitching prospects who have shown upside when on the mound. Didier Fuentes was lights out in relief for Atlanta and should get a chance to start, and River Ryan figures to be in the rotation for the Tigers after being the headliner in the Skubal deal. He has flashed real ability before, but he needs to stay healthy.
| More About Command or Weak Contact | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 67 | Trevor Rogers | Free Agent | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 68 | Troy Melton | DET | No | WHIP guys |
| 69 | Sean Manaea | NYM | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 70 | Michael King | Free Agent | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 71 | Framber Valdez | DET | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 72 | Foster Griffin | Free Agent | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 73 | Emerson Hancock | SEA | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 74 | Jake Bennett | BOS | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 75 | Tyler Mahle | Free Agent | No | WHIP guys |
| 76 | Ranger Suarez | BOS | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 77 | Michael Wacha | KCR | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
These pitchers win with walks and contact, not strikeouts, and many have a Stuff+ under 100 (Tyler Mahle 88, Jake Bennett 93, Ranger Suarez 94, Michael King 95). Some of these guys have been top 30 pitchers before and potentially could again, but the ceiling just doesn’t feel overly high. I would draft this group for innings and WHIP, especially in deeper formats.
| Inconsistent But Has Flashed | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 78 | Robert Gasser | MIL | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 78 | MacKenzie Gore | TEX | No | Strikeouts, command concern |
| 79 | José Soriano | TOR | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
| 80 | Joey Cantillo | CLE | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
| 81 | Will Warren | NYY | No | Young power arms |
| 82 | Tanner Bibee | CLE | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 83 | Connelly Early | WAS | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 84 | Bryce Miller | SEA | Yes | Strikeout guys |
| 85 | Andrew Abbott | CIN | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
Every pitcher here has had a good stretch, but none has strung together a full good year. Some of that is due to injury (Bryce Miller and Connelly Early), but there is just a lot of volatility in this group. Even pitchers that have had good full seasons, like Andrew Abbott, have seemingly never had the profile to back up that success. I do like guys like Early, Miller, Joey Cantillo, or MacKenzie Gore as late-round flyers just in case they can ever put it together or stay healthy.
| Could be a Stud, Could be Demoted | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 87 | Ryan Sloan | SEA | No | Depth prospects, unproven |
| 88 | Hagen Smith | CHW | No | Prospects, command concern |
| 89 | Brandon Sproat | MIL | No | Strikeouts, command concern |
| 90 | Connor Prielipp | MIN | No | Strikeout guys |
| 91 | Shane Drohan | MIL | No | Strikeout guys |
| 92 | Reese Olson | DET | Yes | Strikeout guys |
| 93 | Jack Leiter | TEX | Yes | Strikeouts, command concern |
| 94 | Zebby Matthews | MIN | No | Strikeout guys |
This tier is about uncertainty, and it mixes prospects with young arms who have not settled in. Hagen Smith may be the most interesting. He made his MLB debut as a reliever with a 1.32 ERA, 0.95 WHIP, 37.4% K, 23.4% K-BB, 2.97 SIERA, 14.6% SwStr%, and 108 Stuff+ over 27.1 IP. However, his Triple-A stats were not as good, and he has some major command concerns. Treat this tier as late-round upside.
| Low Upside But a Safe Floor | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 95 | Shane Baz | BAL | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 96 | Merrill Kelly | ARI | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 97 | Matthew Boyd | CHC | No | WHIP guys |
| 98 | Kyle Leahy | STL | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 99 | Michael Soroka | Free Agent | No | WHIP guys |
| 100 | Noah Cameron | KCR | No | WHIP guys |
| 101 | Peter Lambert | HOU | No | Strikeout guys |
| 102 | Justin Wrobleski | LAD | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 103 | Brandon Pfaadt | ARI | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 104 | Dean Kremer | MIN | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 105 | Ryne Nelson | ARI | No | Strikeout guys |
| 106 | Cody Bradford | TEX | No | WHIP guys |
| 107 | Casey Mize | Free Agent | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 108 | Andre Pallante | STL | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
Most of these pitchers will not win you a league, but they are likely to produce solid ratios and good innings totals. Most of these guys feel like streamers or solid targets in 15-team leagues and draft-and-hold formats.
| No Idea What You Are | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 109 | Luis Castillo | CHW | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 110 | Dustin May | Free Agent | No | Strikeout guys |
| 111 | Anthony Kay | CHW | No | Young power arms |
| 112 | Tatsuya Imai | HOU | No | Strikeout guys |
| 113 | Landen Roupp | SFG | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
| 114 | Matthew Liberatore | STL | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 115 | Jacob Lopez | ATH | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
| 116 | Janson Junk | MIA | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 117 | Brayan Bello | BOS | No | Weak contact and durability |
I think the title of this group kind of says it all. I have no idea what to make of most of these guys. Matthew Liberatore had an intriguing stretch in the second half. Janson Junk has a deep pitch mix and a solid Stuff+ grade. Brayan Bello looked like an entirely different pitcher when he moved into the bulk reliever role. I was high on Landen Roupp for much of last year, but the results never came. Maybe we need to see something in spring from this group, or maybe we avoid.
| Are You Healthy? I’m Interested If Yes | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 118 | Kyle Harrison | MIL | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 119 | Justin Steele | CHC | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 120 | Cade Horton | CHC | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 121 | Kris Bubic | Free Agent | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 122 | Edward Cabrera | CHC | Yes | Strikeout, innings concerns |
| 123 | Jack Flaherty | Free Agent | Yes | Flagged, but pitched in 2026 |
| 124 | Clarke Schmidt | NYY | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 125 | Luis Gil | NYY | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 126 | Tylor Megill | NYM | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 127 | AJ Smith-Shawver | ATL | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
All ten of these arms have an injury discount, and the question heading into your fantasy drafts is whether the production will be there when they return. As of now, I can’t draft any of them as more than a late-round dart throw.
| Young Arms But Might Have Rotation Spots | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 128 | Gage Jump | ATH | No | Power arms, command concern |
| 129 | Quinn Mathews | STL | No | Unclassified |
| 130 | David Sandlin | CHW | No | Prospects, command concern |
| 131 | Jonah Tong | NYM | No | Prospects, command concern |
| 132 | George Klassen | LAA | No | Prospects, command concern |
| 133 | Zac Thornton | NYM | No | WHIP guys |
| 134 | Drew Thorpe | CHW | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 135 | Noah Schultz | CHW | No | Young power arms |
| 136 | Blade Tidwell | SFG | No | Rising arms, unproven |
| 137 | J.T. Ginn | ATH | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
Maybe I’m too low on these arms, but I don’t see a lot of security in any of them. All of them have a legit case to be in their team’s starting rotation, but I also see a world where they begin the year in Triple-A. Gage Jump and J.T. Ginn also get dinged for their brutal home park.
| Probably Not Healthy to Begin | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 138 | Spencer Schwellenbach | ATL | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 139 | Cole Ragans | KCR | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 140 | Hunter Greene | CIN | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 141 | David Festa | MIN | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 142 | DJ Herz | WSN | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 143 | Nestor Cortes | Free Agent | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |

| 145 | Bowden Francis | TOR | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 146 | Hurston Waldrep | ATL | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 147 | Ben Brown | CHC | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 148 | Brandon Walter | HOU | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 149 | Zach Eflin | BAL | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
| 150 | Jordan Montgomery | Free Agent | Yes | Missed most of 2026 |
We end with a tier of guys who we feel confident either won’t begin the year healthy or have missed so much time that it’s hard to know what to get from them. I wanted to list them here because the offseason could change how we rank them, but these are not really names to be targeting in your drafts.

item.title: [Bleacher Report] Tarik Skubal and the Next 10 Players to Sign $200 Million Contracts
item.dc:creator: Joel Reuter

item.content:encoded:
Assuming something resembling a normal MLB offseason emerges from the rubble of CBA negotiations this winter, two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal could be in line for a record-setting payday for a pitcher.
At the very least, he's a lock to exceed $200 million in his first trip to free agency. He could be eyeing a $400 million mega deal as one of the best pitchers to ever hit the open market.
There is a steep drop-off in earning power behind him in this year's free-agent class, but there are high-profile extension candidates across baseball, and more and more teams are making an early push to lock up young talent.
Ahead, we've taken a shot at predicting the next 10 players who will sign $200 million contracts, with age, production, long-term outlook and proximity to free agency all factors in building the list.
2B/SS CJ Abrams
1 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2028
Whether he is the centerpiece of a blockbuster deal or a foundational building block for the Nationals, CJ Abrams has put himself in position for a massive payday following a career year offensively.
Still only 26 years old, he posted a 127 OPS+ with 30 doubles, 33 home runs, 106 RBI and 34 steals in a 5.1-WAR season, earning his second All-Star selection in the last three years.
Despite his defensive shortcomings and a potential long-term move to second base, his age and offensive impact make him an obvious candidate for a lucrative extension and the potential headliner of the 2028-29 free-agent class.
Even as a second baseman, he will have a strong case to eclipse the seven-year, $175 million deal that Marcus Semien signed with the Rangers prior to his age-31 season.
DH Yordan Alvarez
2 of 10
Contract Status: Two years, $53.7 million remaining on contract
Teams buying out the final year or two of a superstar's contract to lock him up with a fresh long-term extension is common practice. No one is a more obvious candidate for that approach than presumptive AL MVP Yordan Alvarez.
With two years remaining on his six-year, $115 million extension, and fresh off a season where he hit .316/.432/.601 with 42 home runs and 106 RBI to make a run at AL Triple Crown honors, he is unquestionably one of the game's elite offensive talents.
His back-loaded current deal will pay him $26.8 million in 2027 and 2028, so replacing those two years with a fresh long-term deal and an AAV somewhere in the $30 million range would not actually be tacking that much onto the payroll next year.
The Astros could also decide it's time to rebuild, which would make him a blockbuster trade chip and an obvious extension candidate for any team that ponies up the prospect talent to land him.
3B Junior Caminero
3 of 10
Contract Status: Pre-arbitration, controllable through 2030
Junior Caminero will not reach arbitration for the first time until after the 2027 season. At that point, he might be in line for a record-setting payday if he continues to produce at the level he has in the last two seasons.
2025: 154 G, 130 OPS+, 45 HR, 110 RBI, 4.3 WAR
2026: 162 G, 144 OPS+, 42 HR, 101 RBI, 5.7 WAR
The Rays have never signed a player to a contract worth a guaranteed $200 million, but Caminero is a face-of-the-franchise caliber superstar worth committing a significant chunk of the payroll to for the foreseeable future.
The additional revenue that will come from their World Series trip, coupled with the potential for a salary floor to be instituted in the upcoming CBA negotiations, raises the chances of Caminero inking an extension.
The 11-year, $288.8 million extension Bobby Witt Jr. signed with the Royals is a reasonable starting point in negotiations, but we are inching closer to Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s 14-year, $500 million deal with every ball he sends into the seats.
SS Elly De La Cruz
4 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2029
The Reds have already approached Elly De La Cruz with an extension offer.
"We engaged in Spring Training of 2025 and presented an offer," Reds president of baseball operations Nick Krall told reporters in January. "The offer would have been the largest contract in Reds history. We didn't have any further conversations regarding the offer."
The current largest contract in club history is the 10-year, $225 million deal Joey Votto signed in 2012, so he has already had the opportunity to join the $200 million club and declined.
With Scott Boras as his agent and coming off the best season of his career, in which he showed improved defensive chops alongside his tantalizing power-speed combination, the likelihood of him signing an early extension is extremely low.
The Reds could eventually put him on the trade block if an extension doesn't work out. Any team acquiring him would likely want to get a long-term deal on the books. That provides multiple avenues for a huge payday in the coming years.
RHP Logan Gilbert
5 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2027
The volatility of pitchers makes mega contracts far less common, though Dylan Cease did reel in a seven-year, $210 million payday from the Blue Jays last offseason, even coming off an inconsistent contract year.
Over the last five seasons, Logan Gilbert has averaged 31 starts and 180.1 innings while posting a 3.46 ERA and 110 ERA+. That durability and consistency make him a prime candidate for a massive contract.
His 14.2 WAR over that five-year stretch ranks among the top 20 among all pitchers. Whether it's an extension from the Mariners or as the top arm in the 2027-28 free-agent class, a boatload of money is on the horizon.
The 29-year-old played on a $10.9 million salary last season. He is projected to earn $15.4 million in his final year of arbitration, which would make him an extremely attractive trade chip if Seattle decided to deal from its pitching depth.
SS Gunnar Henderson
6 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2028
In a down year by his own lofty standards, Gunnar Henderson was still a 3.2-WAR player, posting a 102 OPS+ with 57 extra-base hits and 24 home runs while starting 149 games at shortstop.
After a 6.1-WAR rookie season in 2023 and an 8.8-WAR follow-up season in which he finished fourth in AL MVP voting, he firmly established himself as one of the game's brightest young stars.
He looked like a clear long-term building block while the Orioles were on the rise, but their stalled progress toward contention led to the Adley Rutschman trade this past summer. That might not be the end of the roster turnover.
MLB insider Buster Olney made headlines in August when he said, "he's not going to sign there long term in all likelihood," while discussing Henderson's future. Whether he is the next homegrown star out the door or reaches free agency after the 2028 season, he will command big money.
1B Munetaka Murakami
7 of 10
Contract Status: One year, $17.5 million remaining on contract
Despite a prolific run in the Japanese League, Munetaka Murakami was not met with the robust market many expected last offseason due to swing-and-miss concerns. He signed a two-year, $34 million deal with the White Sox. That translated into him becoming the center of their surprising climb to the postseason.
The 26-year-old had a .207 batting average and 35.4 percent strikeout rate, but his on-base ability (16.6 BB%, .347 OBP) and power (130 OPS+, 35 HR) still made him one of the most impactful sluggers in baseball.
If he can match that performance in his second season stateside, a significantly more lucrative contract likely awaits in his next trip to free agency.
Pete Alonso got a $31 million AAV on a five-year deal ahead of his age-31 season as an elite power hitter with limited secondary value. Murakami will be four years younger when he shops for his next contract. Even if he doesn't match that AAV, a longer deal could easily push the full value above $200 million.
SS Jeremy Peña
8 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2027
At first glance, Jeremy Peña is not an obvious candidate for a $200 million deal, but never underestimate the earning power of a quality shortstop in a thin market at the position.
The 29-year-old has taken his offensive game to another level the past two seasons, logging a .291/.345/.477 line and 130 OPS+ despite missing some time to injuries. He remains a standout defender.
With 22.2 WAR over his first five seasons and a playoff track record few players his age can match, he would be an obvious extension candidate if not for the fact that he switched agents and hired Scott Boras in June 2025.
That clearly indicates he intends to test the market after the 2027 season, which could put him on the trade block this winter. Xander Bogaerts was the same age when he signed his 11-year, $280 million contract with the Padres. While he had a longer track record, Peña is a far superior defender.
LHP Tarik Skubal
9 of 10
Contract Status: Free agent
Tarik Skubal was the only 2026-27 free agent projected to earn a contract north of $200 million in my recent article predicting the 10 biggest contracts handed out in free agency this winter.
The nine-year, $324 million contract that Gerrit Cole signed prior to the 2020 season is a logical starting point, but Skubal could be aiming for a $40 million AAV given his track record and the rising cost of frontline pitching.
Barring a surprise mega-deal for Japanese League star Teruaki Sato, the odds are extremely high that Skubal will be the next free agent to lock in at least $200 million.
With a 2.42 ERA, 0.92 WHIP and 655 strikeouts in 546 innings over the last three seasons, he has firmly established himself as one of the best pitchers in the sport in the prime of his career.
OF James Wood
10 of 10
Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible through 2030
One of the key return pieces from the Juan Soto blockbuster trade with the Padres, James Wood has developed into one of the best young sluggers in baseball and the face of the franchise for the Nationals.
The towering 6'6" outfielder has put together consecutive 30-homer, 3-WAR seasons. This year, he quietly developed into a more complete hitter beneath the surface of his 144 OPS+ and 30 long balls.
The 24-year-old raised his walk rate (12.3 to 16.4 percent), lowered his strikeout rate (32.1 to 28.7 percent) and added 21 steals in 25 attempts without sacrificing any of his power production.
After signing Cade Cavalli to a four-year, $47 million extension in September, the Nationals could be looking to lock up more pieces this offseason. Wood is the top candidate for a franchise cornerstone-level deal.

item.title: [NBC Sports] 2027 Fantasy Baseball Mock Draft: Can you trust Garrett Crochet in 2027? What about Byron Buxton?
