item.content:encoded:
The 2026 MLB Postseason is entering the Championship Series, but the time for fantasy baseball analysis never truly stops. Last Monday, we started our Rotoworld Staff and Friends Fantasy Baseball Mock Draft for the 2027 season. While many places do a “too early” mock draft, we’d argue that it’s not really too early to look ahead to next season. I’ve been posting a collection of “look back” articles reviewing the best picks of the 2026 season, the worst picks, and my key lessons, but all of these articles are linked together by the idea that immediately taking stock in the season, before the offseason hype starts to creep in, can be an incredibly valuable experience.
So we invited our staff and a few of our friends to put together a 15-round mock draft that we’ll complete over the next couple of weeks and continue to break down for you in chunks over on our site. Today you’ll get the first four rounds, and then I’ll be back to update the next four or five rounds by the end of the week and then do one more update at the end.
We hope you find it a useful tool, and we’ll see how much it changes over the next few weeks.
2027 Fantasy Baseball Mock Draft
| Round 1 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 1 | RotoPat (Rotoworld) | Shohei Ohtani | UT/SP | LAD |
| 2 | George Bissell (Rotoworld) | Pete Crow-Armstrong | OF | CHC |
| 3 | Frank Stampfl (CBS Sports) | Bobby Witt Jr. | SS | KC |
| 4 | D.J. Short (Rotoworld) | Elly De La Cruz | SS | CIN |
| 5 | Scott Pianowski (Yahoo Sports) | Fernando Tatis Jr. | 2B/OF | SD |
| 6 | Rivers McCown (Rotoworld) | Junior Caminero | 3B | TB |
| 7 | Matthew Pouliot (Rotoworld) | Aaron Judge | OF | NYY |
| 8 | Dave Shovein (Rotoworld) | Juan Soto | OF | NYM |
| 9 | Frank Ammirante (RotoBaller) | Jackson Chourio | OF | MIL |
| 10 | James Schiano (Rotoworld) | James Wood | OF | WSH |
| 11 | Justin Mason (FanGraphs) | Yordan Alvarez | OF | HOU |
| 12 | Jorge Montanez (Rotoworld) | Ben Rice | 1B | NYY |
Perhaps the story here is that no starting pitchers went in the first 12 picks. One season after Tarik Skubal, Garrett Crochet, and Paul Skenes either got hurt or had down seasons, none of the drafters seemed willing to roll the dice on a starting pitcher with their first pick. Honestly, I can’t blame them. Early-round hitters, on average, continue to out-produce early-round pitchers at similar draft costs. The pitchers that do hit can make a huge difference for your team, but the risk is exponentially higher. A hitter taken here who fails to produce value, like Kyle Tucker this year, can still produce $10 of value, but a pitcher who goes in the first round and fails to produce value is almost always due to injury, and they can give you no value.
We did see Pat still choose Shohei Ohtani (dual position eligible here) as the top pick over Pete Crow-Armstrong. There are certainly some questions as to whether or not Ohtani’s body can hold up to a whole season as a starting pitcher and a DH, which will bring some uncertainty to his fantasy value. We also know he’s clearly not healthy right now, so we’ll need to see if any of these injuries require offseason surgery, but PCA has certainly worked his way into the conversation to be first overall.
A big surprise for some might be seeing Fernando Tatis Jr. this high. The Padres outfielder was one of the best hitters in baseball from June 1st on after a batting stance change allowed him to clear his hips more easily and unlock the pull-side power that we know he has. He also picked up 2B eligibility this season, which will be huge for him at a pretty barren position.
Jackson Chourio and James Wood have used breakout seasons to propel them into the first-round conversation, and you have to wonder if there is yet another level of development there, and Yordan Alvarez now has outfield eligibility in all formats, which makes him an even safer pick here. There look to be plenty of outfield options in the first round, including injured New York stars Juan Soto and Aaron Judge. Both of them being in the first round makes sense, but we may start to have to ask real questions about Judge’s durability. He’ll be 35 years old next season. He’s a giant human being, and the strain of playing the outfield every day at that size takes a real toll on your body. The fact that his two major injuries this season were both soft tissue or muscle injuries (and not a broken toe) should begin to raise some questions about whether or not we can count on 150+ games from Judge going forward.
His teammate, Ben Rice, used a 40-home run season to catapult him into the first round as well. That’s without catcher eligibility. Rice was the first 1B off the board in this draft, and I really find it hard to argue against that. Some guys in the next round have an argument, but Rice is a tremendous overall hitter. He has clear power. He plays in a great park for his approach, and there is no way the Yankees are going back to regularly sitting him against lefties. Even if Rice is more of a mid-30s home run hitter going forward than a true 40+ guy, his approach at the plate makes me feel good about his contact and batting average, and that puts him ahead of the guys who will follow him in round two.
| Round 2 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 13 | Jorge Montanez | CJ Abrams | SS/2B | WSH |
| 14 | Justin Mason | Jose Ramirez | 3B | CLE |
| 15 | James Schiano | Jacob Misiorowski | SP | MIL |
| 16 | Frank Ammirante | Tarik Skubal | SP | LAD |
| 17 | Dave Shovein | Ronald Acuña Jr. | OF | ATL |
| 18 | Matthew Pouliot | Nick Kurtz | 1B | OAK |
| 19 | Rivers McCown | Jordan Walker | OF | STL |
| 20 | Scott Pianowski | Kyle Schwarber | DH | PHI |
| 21 | D.J. Short | Pete Alonso | 1B | BAL |
| 22 | Frank Stampfl | Corbin Carroll | OF | ARI |
| 23 | George Bissell | Cam Schlittler | SP | NYY |
| 24 | Roto Pat | Yoshinobu Yamamoto | SP | LAD |
And now the pitchers start to come off the board. Not really a surprise with who the first three arms were off the board: Jacob Misiorowski, Tarik Skubal, and Cam Schlittler. I assume those will be the top three arms in pretty much all rankings heading into 2027. Pat did snag Yoshinobu Yamamoto as the fourth starter picked in this round, and while some may argue for Chris Sale or Cristopher Sanchez here, there’s a strong case that Yamamoto could be locked into the fourth spot. There is still some elevated risk with starting pitchers in the second round, but at least every one of these teams added an elite bat in the first round, and both George and Pat were able to take second elite bats at the start of the third round, so this risk feels more palatable.
CJ Abrams is another player, like Tatis Jr., who picked up second base eligibility in most formats. That’s huge for his fantasy value. So is hitting .261 with 33 home runs and 34 steals while driving in 106 runs. Abrams will be 26 years old next season, and while his future in Washington is a bit cloudy, he’s an elite offensive talent who is finally making good on that promise.
We had some former first-round picks fall into the second with Jose Ramirez, Ronald Acuña Jr., and Corbin Carroll all falling into the second round. The falls make sense too. Ramirez and Acuña Jr. now just have a bit more injury risk than some of the other players going in the first round. Ramirez still has great upside at a position that lacks talent, which may drive his price up, but he’ll be 34 years old, and he hit just 12 home runs and batted .235 this year after hamate surgery. Are you willing to bet that he gets back to 100% of his old self, or do we think it’s more likely that he’ll be 75-80% of the guy who almost went 40/40 in 2024? Acuña Jr. is a harder bet because he has now played under 108 games in three straight seasons and has played over 120 games once since 2019. It’s hard to bet on a full season of production, and with PCA, Chourio, and James Wood emerging, it makes sense to go with the younger/healthier players.
At the same position, the most interesting name in this round is probably Jordan Walker. He had a breakout season this year, hitting .269 with 29 home runs, 102 RBI, and 22 steals. He also just turned 24 years old, so there is plenty of growth still possible for him. He struggled through an injury at the end of the year, which hurt his September stats, but there will be no half measures with Walker in 2027. You have to either be all-in on the fact that 2026 was a real breakout for a former top prospect or just acknowledge that you won’t be getting him in your drafts.
Pete Alonso and Nick Kurtz are the two first basemen I alluded to earlier who land here in round 2. Kurtz played just 99 games this season due to injury but still hit 21 home runs while batting .256. We know the hitting environment in Sacramento is elite, so he should still be going in this range.
| Round 3 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 25 | Roto Pat | Sal Stewart | 1B | CIN |
| 26 | George Bissell | Konnor Griffin | SS | PIT |
| 27 | Frank Stampfl | Miguel Vargas | 3B | CHW |
| 28 | D.J. Short | Cristopher Sanchez | SP | PHI |
| 29 | Scott Pianowski | Paul Skenes | SP | PIT |
| 30 | Rivers McCown | Mason Miller | RP | SD |
| 31 | Matthew Pouliot | Julio Rodriguez | OF | SEA |
| 32 | Dave Shovein | Trea Turner | SS | PHI |
| 33 | Frank Ammirante | Gunnar Henderson | SS | BAL |
| 34 | James Schiano | Jackson Merrill | OF | SD |
| 35 | Justin Mason | Kevin McGonigle | SS/3B | DET |
| 36 | Jorge Montanez | Jesus Luzardo | SP | PHI |
We see three current-year rookies go in Round 3, announcing themselves as top-tier talents for years to come, and it’s hard to argue against it. Sal Stewart, Konnor Griffin, and Kevin McGonigle all showed that they can handle this level of competition, and we should expect more growth from these young players. The same goes for Miguel Vargas, who is not a rookie but broke out in 2026 in a way that suggests consistent value. He’s always had an elite plate approach, and now he added pull-side power to that equation. Vargas will be 27 years old and is in an ascending lineup, so he belongs in this range.
We saw the next group of starting pitchers go with Cristopher Sanchez, Paul Skenes, and Jesus Luzardo. Obviously, the name everybody will want to talk about is Skenes. It was a bad year for the Pirates ace, and while he claimed he wasn’t hurt, his velocity fell throughout the year, and he was not missing as many bats. There had been some previous concerns that his fastball wasn’t a huge whiff pitch to righties (10.7% swinging strike rate in 2025), but Skenes saw huge strides there this season. However, that was basically the only place he got better, and by elevating his four-seamer more for whiffs, he also started to allow more hard contact. It’s hard to see Skenes being this bad again, but we also can’t ignore how this season went.
Mason Miller went here as the first closer off the board, and three former first-round picks fell in Gunnar Henderson, Trea Turner, and Julio Rodriguez. I covered Gunnar and Trea in my article on what I learned from the 2026 fantasy baseball season, so you should read that, but essentially their 2025 price baked in a full return to peak value and ignored the warning signs from that season. We don’t appear to be doing that this year.
| Round 4 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 37 | Jorge Montanez | Drew Rasmussen | SP | TB |
| 38 | Justin Mason | Chris Sale | SP | ATL |
| 39 | James Schiano | Francisco Lindor | SS | NYM |
| 40 | Frank Ammirante | Kyle Tucker | OF | LAD |
| 41 | Dave Shovein | Brice Turang | 2B | MIL |
| 42 | Matthew Pouliot | Zach Neto | SS | LAA |
| 43 | Rivers McCown | Oneil Cruz | OF | PIT |
| 44 | Scott Pianowski | Matt Olson | 1B | ATL |
| 45 | D.J. Short | Carson Benge | OF | NYM |
| 46 | Frank Stampfl | Chase Burns | SP | CIN |
| 47 | George Bissell | Hunter Goodman | C | COL |
| 48 | Roto Pat | Nolan McLean | SP | NYM |
Now we answer the question of how far Kyle Tucker falls as Frank Ammirante takes him with the fourth pick in the fourth round, 40th overall. I covered Tucker more extensively in my article revisiting the top two rounds of 2025 drafts, but the miss on Tucker was essentially looking at pedigree (his seasons before his last two injured ones) and also the team context (a move to the Dodgers) and ignoring that he hadn’t had a fully productive year in a while. I’m not sure anybody expected that Tucker would see his barrel-rate collapse and that he would make uncharacteristically aggressive, out-of-character swing decisions, so perhaps we can expect a slight bounce back to his previously healthy form.
Four more starting pitchers go off the board here, and it’s an interesting group. Drew Rasmussen was brilliant this season, but it was also his first over 150 innings, and he’s had three elbow surgeries. Can you bank on his health as your ace? Kind of the same question for Chris Sale, who will be 38 next year and has basically alternated healthy years with injured years. After being hurt for basically all of 2021-23, he threw 178 innings in 2024, then 125 in 2025, and then 163 this year. What’s in store for 2027?
The final two arms were young pitchers in Chase Burns and Nolan McLean. The Burns pick makes sense given his elite strikeout upside and plus raw stuff, but McLean is harder to see here. Not that he’s a bad pitcher, but taking him as the 11th starting pitcher is assuming tons of growth. His 26% strikeout rate and 16.6% K-BB% don’t line up with some of the elite arms in this range, and his 10.5% swinging strike rate continues to suggest some concern with his ability to consistently miss bats. He’ll be 26 next year, and he’s clearly a talented arm, but taking him this high means he really HAS to take the next step, or he won’t return value.
Oneil Cruz’s bounce-back season pushed him up into the fourth round, and he’s joined by young outfielder Carson Benge, who hit .282 with 20 home runs and 22 steals in his rookie season. He didn’t get the fanfare of the other rookies who went higher in this draft, but Benge has a true five-category skill set and should be in an improved lineup next season.
We also saw our first catcher go off the board in Hunter Goodman. Keep in mind that this is a one-catcher format, which is why you’re not seeing a lot of catchers go early, but George wanted to lock up an elite bat at the position. With Ben Rice no longer catcher eligible, Goodman was the top fantasy catcher this season after hitting 41 home runs, driving in 88 runs, and hitting .245 in Coors Field. There’s little reason to believe he can’t do it again.
| Round 5 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 49 | Roto Pat | Rafael Devers | 1B | SF |
| 50 | George Bissell | Cade Smith | RP | CLE |
| 51 | Frank Stampfl | Zack Wheeler | SP | PHI |
| 52 | D.J. Short | Parker Messick | SP | CLE |
| 53 | Scott Pianowski | Randy Arozarena | OF | SEA |
| 54 | Rivers McCown | Dylan Cease | SP | TOR |
| 55 | Matthew Pouliot | Vladimir Guerrero Jr. | 1B | TOR |
| 56 | Dave Shovein | Logan Gilbert | SP | SEA |
| 57 | Frank Ammirante | Garrett Crochet | SP | BOS |
| 58 | James Schiano | Bryce Harper | 1B/OF | PHI |
| 59 | Justin Mason | Logan Henderson | SP | MIL |
| 60 | Jorge Montanez | Michael Harris II | OF | ATL |
A few big-name starting pitchers with major injuries go in this round. Zack Wheeler (SP12) missed half of this past season after having thoracic outlet surgery, Garrett Crochet (SP16) missed basically the whole season with a shoulder injury, Dylan Cease (SP14) ended the season on the injured list with a shoulder injury, and Logan Henderson (SP17) has missed time in each of the last two seasons with injuries. We’re now outside of the top 10 starting pitchers, so these guys don’t HAVE to be your ace, but this is still an early round draft pick for pitchers who have some overall health concerns. I understand the argument for their upside, and while I may not make the pick here, that’s just my personal drafting philosophy.
Parker Messick (SP13) and Logan Gilbert (SP15) also go in this round. Both of them feel a bit safer from a health standpoint, and there is still an argument that Gilbert has another level of production to hit. I have him as a top-10 starting pitcher, so I like him going as the 15th starter off the board.
We see Cade Smith go here as the second closer off the board, and Rafael Devers and Bryce Harper make sense in this range as veteran 1B who are likely past their peak but continue to produce overall solid numbers. Devers really turned things around after a slow start to the year and seems as consistent as ever.
We also see two outfielders coming off big seasons in Michael Harris II and Randy Arozarena. James Schiano and I actually discussed this exact either-or in a video we recorded after the Braves were eliminated from the postseason. I picked Harris II easily because I believe in the changes he’s made over the last year-and-a-half, and I’m not looking to pay for Arozarena’s career year.
Lastly, we need to address Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who finally goes off the board here in the fifth. We all know how Vlad Jr. struggled this year, but he’s now going as the sixth 1B, late in the fifth round, which is way more palatable for me. I know the power wasn’t there, but we have enough of a track record to feel confident that he is at least a 20-25 home run bat who can hit .280 in what should be a solid lineup. That’s still a solid fantasy asset; it’s just not a pick to make in the first three rounds of your draft. Also, getting corrective eye surgery can’t be bad either.
| Round 6 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 61 | Jorge Montanez | Jac Caglianone | OF | KC |
| 62 | Justin Mason | Jhoan Duran | RP | PHI |
| 63 | James Schiano | Jazz Chisholm Jr. | OF | NYY |
| 64 | Frank Ammirante | Cal Raleigh | C | SEA |
| 65 | Dave Shovein | Andres Munoz | RP | SEA |
| 66 | Matthew Pouliot | Bryan Woo | SP | SEA |
| 67 | Rivers McCown | Drake Baldwin | C | ATL |
| 68 | Scott Pianowski | Alex Bregman | 3B | CHC |
| 69 | D.J. Short | Gavin Williams | SP | CLE |
| 70 | Frank Stampfl | Shea Langeliers | C | OAK |
| 71 | George Bissell | Kade Anderson | SP | SEA |
| 72 | Roto Pat | Wyatt Langford | OF | TEX |
This is a super interesting round to me, and I can’t make much sense of it, haha. There seem to be no runs here or any real trend.
We do get more catchers off the board here with Cal Raleigh, Drake Baldwin, and Shea Langeliers. It feels a little early to be in a one-catcher format, but everybody has their own strategy. Baldwin feels like a great pick after his 2026 season, and while I do think Raleigh is going to bounce back after a down 2026 season, I’m not sure he’d be the gamble I take this early in the sixth round. Yes, you might be getting 30+ home runs from that spot, but the batting average will be a drain, and we have no idea if that lineup will be any good.
Jhoan Duran goes off the board as the third closer, and then Andres Munoz next was a bit of a surprise. He wasn’t really in a closer committee in Seattle this year; they just didn’t get a lot of saves. His SIERA and underlying metrics look a lot better than his ERA, so it does feel like he was just unlucky, but I’m not that convinced the Mariners will be that good next year, and Munoz has never delivered as a consistent top 5-8 closer.
Three risky hitters with plenty of upside also go in this round: Jac Caglianone, Jazz Chisholm Jr., and Wyatt Langford. We don’t really know where Jazz will be next year, but it seems like it won’t be New York. That’s likely a big park downgrade for him. His batting average also regressed pretty drastically this season, which had been a concern for him in previous years. We know the speed will always be there, so he’ll need to land in a park where the power can come as well, but this feels like a fair spot for him. Caglianone is also a popular breakout pick because his batted ball data has been really strong. I like the idea of him taking a big step next season, but a top-60 pick does feel like you’re paying as if the breakthrough is a given. We all know the deal with Langford at this point too. A top-70 pick on him feels right if he can stay healthy, but can he ever stay healthy?
Bryan Woo at SP18 and Gavin Williams at SP19 feel like strong picks at this point. Both of them have immense strikeout upside and the ability to be top-10 starting pitchers. Woo had a bad stretch this season but seemed to right the ship at the end of the year, and Williams still seems to have one iffy inning every game where his command gets wonky. However, the big surprise here was Kade Anderson. I know he was an elite pitching prospect, but he doesn’t have elite MLB velocity or Stuff+, which means that he gets by with command and a deep enough pitch mix. I think he will be a solid starting pitcher, but I’m not sure I see the ceiling to take him as SP20, especially in what will be his rookie season.
| Round 7 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 73 | Roto Pat | Henry Bolte | OF | OAK |
| 74 | George Bissell | Riley Greene | OF | DET |
| 75 | Frank Stampfl | Andy Pages | OF | LAD |
| 76 | D.J. Short | William Contreras | C | MIL |
| 77 | Scott Pianowski | Ceddanne Rafaela | OF | BOS |
| 78 | Rivers McCown | Byron Buxton | OF | MIN |
| 79 | Matthew Pouliot | Ketel Marte | 2B | ARI |
| 80 | Dave Shovein | Max Fried | SP | NYY |
| 81 | Frank Ammirante | Manny Machado | 3B | SD |
| 82 | James Schiano | Payton Tolle | SP | BOS |
| 83 | Justin Mason | Seiya Suzuki | OF | CHC |
| 84 | Jorge Montanez | Josh Hader | RP | HOU |
Round 7 gave us quite the run on outfielders. After Wyatt Langford ended last round, Henry Bolte, Riley Greene, Andy Pages, Ceddanne Rafaela, Byron Buxton, and Seiya Suzuki all came off the board in the seventh round. Bolte is the name that probably stands out. The Athletics’ rookie hit .277/.359/.405 in 119 big league games with 11 home runs and 21 steals. In 65 games in the second half, Bolte hit .289/.370/.448 with eight of his home runs and a 9.2% barrel rate. Bolte has always had loud raw tools, but he has struggled to lift the ball consistently, which has limited his power output. We started to see that a little more from him in the second half and, if it carries over, he has the makings of a 20/30 hitter in a great ballpark. Pat taking him at 73 means Bolte kind of HAS to get close to that in order to return value, which makes the pick a bit of a risk but not one without some logic to it.
The Buxton and Suzuki picks have their own risk too, along with clear upside. Buxton, who was coming off his best season in years, was limited to just 93 games because of a hip injury that ultimately required surgery. He’ll be 33 years old next season, with just one season over 105 games played since 2017 and coming off major hip surgery. A bit on him inside the top 80 is a huge risk, but we also know Buxton can produce fantasy value in 80-100 games. Suzuki is less of an injury risk but more of a team context risk since we have no idea where he’ll be playing next year. Perhaps it could provide a boost to his home run potential. Maybe the team context will limit his counting stats. We won’t know that for a while.
Two more starting pitchers also go here in Max Fried (SP21) and Payton Tolle (SP22), and, spoiler alert, one of them looks like a huge steal. When my starting pitching rankings come out later this week, I will have Tolle in my top 10 starting pitchers. He’ll be slotted right ahead of a tier of aces who have a history of injury (Crochet, Sale, deGrom, Wheeler), so maybe you want to call Tolle a top 15 starter if you’d take all of those injury risks over him. Still, getting a potential top 15 starting pitcher with pick 82 is tremendous. In case you think top-15 is rich for Tolle, he finished as the SP25 this season, and that was while recording just nine wins in 26 starts. He had a 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, and 28.4% strikeout rate and will be just 24 years old next season. As his breaking balls continue to develop, his performance should only improve.
| Round 8 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 85 | Jorge Montanez | Zack Gelof | 2B/OF | OAK |
| 86 | Justin Mason | Chase DeLauter | OF | CLE |
| 87 | James Schiano | Aroldis Chapman | RP | BOS |
| 88 | Frank Ammirante | Hunter Brown | SP | HOU |
| 89 | Dave Shovein | Freddie Freeman | 1B | LAD |
| 90 | Matthew Pouliot | Louis Varland | RP | TOR |
| 91 | Rivers McCown | Mason Montgomery | RP | PIT |
| 92 | Scott Pianowski | Mookie Betts | SS | LAD |
| 93 | D.J. Short | Tyler Soderstrom | 1B/OF | OAK |
| 94 | Frank Stampfl | Bryan Baker | RP | TB |
| 95 | George Bissell | Grant Taylor | RP | CHW |
| 96 | Roto Pat | JJ Wetherholt | SS | STL |
After Josh Hader went off the board in the last round as RP5, we got a run on closers here in the eighth round with Aroldis Chapman (RP6), Louis Varland (RP7), Mason Montgomery (RP8), Bryan Baker (RP9), and Grant Taylor (RP10). Hader and Chapman are the two established names among the group and make clear sense here, and Baker tied for the MLB lead in saves this season and will return for the potential World Series champion Rays. I’d say that makes him a solid top-ten closer. The other three are all bets on upside, and all bets that make sense. Varland was electric as a closer for the Blue Jays this season and finished as RP3 on the year. Taylor and Montgomery weren’t even full-time closers, and they finished as RP6 and RP7, respectively, due to their high innings totals and strikeout rates. The potential issue for both Taylor and Montgomery is that we have no idea if they will be used as traditional closers. Montgomery feels like the better bet since he had 18 saves this season, but it also took the Pirates a while to turn the role over to him, and they may prefer him in the “fireman” role in the same way the White Sox seem to prefer Taylor. That said, both of them are dominant relief arms.
Three young hitters also went in this round with Zack Gelof, Chase DeLauter, and JJ Wetherholt. Wetherholt as a top 100 pick after his rookie season makes sense, and DeLauter also clearly has the profile of a top 10 pick. His issue has been, and always will be, health risk. Yet, he did manage to play 133 games this season, hitting .287/.363/.457 with 16 home runs and 11 steals. The hard-hit rates suggest that more power could be coming if he can lift the ball a bit more consistently.
Jorge’s pick of Gelof is also a bet that the 26-year-old really did reinvent himself this season, when he hit .256/.322/.475 with 22 home runs and 16 steals in 111 games. Gelof chased less outside of the zone, took a more patient approach overall, made more contact than he ever has, and was less pull-happy than he had been previously. All of that seems to suggest very real growth. Can the growth hold? That will be the big question you have to ask yourself if you draft him in the top 85 picks next season.
We also saw Hunter Brown go off the board here as SP23. If you had told people in March that you’d get Hunter Brown near the end of the eighth round, it would have seemed like a major coup. However, the Astros ace returned from a shoulder injury this season and never looked like himself. Is the injury still lingering, or was 2025 a bit of a fluke? Remember that he had a 3.49 ERA, 1.27 WHIP, and 25% strikeout rate in 2024. There was a major jump forward in 2025, but much of that was in the first half of the season. Even though his ratios remained strong after the All-Star break in 2025, his strikeout rate fell to 24%. So maybe Brown is more of a low 3.00-ERA pitcher who will post a 26% strikeout rate. That’s not a bad profile, but it’s not a top 15 arm. Then you have the health questions to factor in as well, so his slide here makes a bit of sense to me.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Tarik Skubal Rumors Begin With 6 Landing Spots, Including Blue Jays
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: The Tarik Skubal sweepstakes is going to have the attention of fans around Major League Baseball over the next few months until the lefty superstar likely lands a historic deal in free agency. Skubal, the two-time American League Cy Young Award winner, has been the most dominant pitcher in baseball over the last few years and he's going to get paid like it. item.content:encoded:
The Tarik Skubal sweepstakes is going to have the attention of fans around Major League Baseball over the next few months until the lefty superstar likely lands a historic deal in free agency.
Skubal, the two-time American League Cy Young Award winner, has been the most dominant pitcher in baseball over the last few years and he's going to get paid like it. Skubal is just 29 years old and the early rumors and buzz around his sweepstakes have been wild. The current record for the largest contract ever given to a starting pitcher is $325 million given to Yoshinobu Yamamoto. Skubal's market very well could surpass that this winter. Yamamoto was a few years younger when he got that deal, but he also had never thrown a pitch in the majors at the time.
Skubal has thrown plenty. Whoever lands him is going to have to open up the checkbook and hand him a lot of cash. But they will also be getting an ace at the top of the rotation that is nearly unhittable most of the time. But where will he go? MLB.com's Mark Feinsand broke down his market and floated six potential landing spots: Los Angeles Dodgers, Detroit Tigers, New York Mets, Chicago Cubs, Toronto Blue Jays and the Philadelphia Phillies.
Let's break down this information.
Best Landing Spot: New York Mets
Love them or hate them, baseball is better in general when the Mets are good. Pitching is an area where New York needs a facelift in. The Mets also need a new first baseman, but that's another story. If New York landed Skubal, he would be the ace that it has been chasing for a long time. New York is New York. If you can make the Mets good, it would be good for the sport in general.
Worst Landing Spot: Los Angeles Dodgers
This couldn't be more obvious. Part of the reason for the heightened nature of the labor negotiations is hard feelings across the league over the Dodgers' spending. If the Dodgers turn around and hand Skubal a historic deal, it would be the outcome that gets fans around the league the most fired up.
Most Fun Landing Spot: Toronto Blue Jays
The Blue Jays had a bad 2026 season, but this is a club that pushed the Dodgers to Game 7 of the 2025 World Series. Toronto signed Dylan Cease last year and he was awesome throughout the campaign. Injuries dismantled the Blue Jays' rotation, though. The Blue Jays always try to sign the biggest star of the offseason. This year it's Skubal. If Toronto could get a deal done, it would have the best rotation in baseball on paper.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick also received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Fastball On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.title: [fansided.com] Ranking Tarik Skubal suitors from favorites to dark horses
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
item.description: Tarik Skubal and the Los Angeles Dodgers were swept out of the NLCS by the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers, a refreshing change of pace after two years of Dodgers dominance — and a helpful reminder to the MLB owners that payroll alone does not determine winning. It also leaves Skubal with a more difficult decision in free agency than many expected. The Dodgers will not re-sign Skubal before the lockout in December, as there's simply too much risk without knowing how the salary cap will function come 2
item.content:encoded:
Tarik Skubal and the Los Angeles Dodgers were swept out of the NLCS by the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers, a refreshing change of pace after two years of Dodgers dominance — and a helpful reminder to the MLB owners that payroll alone does not determine winning. It also leaves Skubal with a more difficult decision in free agency than many expected.
The Dodgers will not re-sign Skubal before the lockout in December, as there's simply too much risk without knowing how the salary cap will function come 2027. Really regardless of how MLB's labor dispute plays out, however, Los Angeles will hope to retain Skubal, who is still rightly regarded as the most bankable ace in baseball. The question is: Are the Dodgers the favorites for his services? Let's rank all realistic suitors, from least to most realistic.
8. Philadelphia Phillies
The Phillies are desperate and the Phillies typically spend money. Not necessarily as liberally as fans would like, but it's not impossible to imagine Dave Dombrowski — with the World Series window closing rapidly on this aging core — deciding that Skubal is worth an all-in push.
It would give Philadelphia the most talented rotation in MLB between Skubal, Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sánchez, Jesús Luzardo and Aaron Nola, four of whom could compete for NL Cy Young next season. There's also Andrew Painter, a former top prospect who came into his own down the stretch and delivered big outs in the postseason, to provide depth.
The Phillies probably have enough money wrapped up in that rotation (and in Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Trea Turner) to be turned off of paying Skubal top dollar, but it's a fun thought for a team hoping to lean even more on run prevention moving forward.
7. Boston Red Sox
The Red Sox wielded one of the deepest and most reliable rotations in MLB last season; that was with top ace Garrett Crochet on the IL. Upon Crochet's return, Boston will have a compelling blend of experience (Crochet, Ranger Suárez) and emerging youth (Payton Tolle, Jake Bennett) to throw at their opponents.
Then again, they know the toll injuries can take, and Sonny Gray — probably their best regular season starter this past season — is now a free agent. The Red Sox could simply line up a new contract for Gray and be content, but why not aim higher? Skubal has proven remarkably durable over the years and he offers Boston a much longer window as Crochet's partner in crime. Suddenly, the Red Sox have the best one-two punch in baseball and it wouldn't be especially close.
After the Yankees lit them up in the Wild Card round (and after Boston's top arms couldn't pitch deep into either postseason game), there's pressure for a big swing.
6. Chicago Cubs
There's no doubting the Cubs' ability to generate offense, but the rotation has been a sore spot for years now. Jed Hoyer has shown a great appetite for spending in free agency of late; the Alex Bregman signing was a real flex. That said, Chicago needs to allocate more resources toward pitching. The Edward Cabrera trade went belly up. Shōta Imanaga is a free agent now, as are trade deadline pickups Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes.
Chicago will get help internally with both Cade Horton and Justin Steele returning from season-long elbow injuries; Ben Brown, who finally broke out in 2026, should also be back in the mix. Beyond them, however, it's pretty grim. Matthew Boyd and Javier Assad can eat innings in the regular season, but neither has proven able to pitch deep in October — at least not consistently.
Skubal would deliver Chicago the frontline ace it has long lacked, with a solid scaffolding of talent behind him. The Cubs would be much better positioned to challenge Milwaukee in the division and potentially emerge from a crowded National League field.
5. Detroit Tigers
Skubal has made it clear he would've spent his entire career in Detroit if it was up to him. All the Tigers need to do is come through with a competitive offer. While last year's surprise Framber Valdez signing was a positive indication of the front office's competitive intent, there's a reason no Skubal extension ever came to fruition — or even remotely close.
A client of Scott Boras, Skubal was never inclined to sign an extension. But the Tigers' offers weren't even in the parking lot, much less the ballpark. Detroit will need to scale up its ambition significantly if it wants to lure Skubal back to the midwest.
All that said, Skubal has an affection for Detroit that's worth mentioning. The Tigers also desperately need a frontline ace in Skubal's mold. Young bucks like Troy Melton, Keider Montero, Jackson Jobe and River Ryan are very talented, but the Tigers don't really have an established vet besides Valdez, who was a mess last season.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees tend to flex their muscles in free agency, although with diminishing returns in recent years. New York is no longer the most lucrative destination for a lot of A-tier stars. Juan Soto a couple years ago, Kyle Tucker last winter; the Yankees are getting outbid pretty consistently these days. That has not stopped New York from stockpiling stars, though, especially in the rotation.
It would require Hal Steinbrenner and the front office to basically sign off on a blank check, but the Yankees' ALDS loss to the Rays was a sobering defeat. There are cracks in the foundation. Many of those cracks are injury-related and concentrated in the lineup; Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón is as strong a four-man gauntlet as any rotation in MLB. The Yankees also have Ryan Weathers, Will Warren and top prospects like Elmer Rodríguez and Carlos Lagrange for depth.
Still, the Yankees know the importance of depth, especially as their non-Schlittler core ages and becomes more injury-prone. Skubal provides stability and instantly lends credibility to any postseason aspirations. Schlittler-Skubal becomes the most fearsome pitching duo in baseball. Never say never.
3. Toronto Blue Jays
The Blue Jays have steadily become the most aggressive front office in the American League. After finishing runner-up in the Juan Soto and Shohei Ohtani sweepstakes, Toronto extended Vladimir Guerrero Jr. at a $500 million price point and signed Dylan Cease in the early days of free agency last winter. A disappointing season should not preclude Toronto from maintaining its all-in approach; if anything, it's more motivation for the Blue Jays to stack talent. This team was in the World Series a year ago.
Toronto is a great market, with a vibrant local culture and an entire country behind the Blue Jays. That ought to appeal to the vanity of a star like Skubal, who would team up with the projected AL Cy Young runner-up in Cease. The Jays also made a savvy trade for José Soriano at the deadline, adding another premium arm in his prime. Trey Yesavage, once healthy, could resume his ascent to stardom. The talent is there.
Skubal solidifies Toronto as a legitimate World Series contender coming into 2027. Moreover, the Jays have a lot of money coming off the books, which should free up the front office to spend recklessly where it counts. Toronto is always the "dark horse" in these top-dollar bidding wars, but ruling out the Blue Jays would be foolish.
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
It's impossible to rule out the incumbents. Los Angeles made the Skubal trade in part because of their deep farm system — and in part because it set the stage for a potential long-term partnership. There's a reason small-market front offices were unwilling to match L.A.'s outgoing package (see: Brewers). The Dodgers could afford to trade two of the 50ish best prospects in baseball because the team can feel reasonably good about both competing for a World Series this season (oh well) and re-signing Skubal when he hits the open market.
An NLCS loss does complicate the situation somewhat, not to mention the unknowability of upcoming labor disputes. The Dodgers' loss was a direct result of investing hundreds of millions of dollars in stars who are beginning to decline. Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Shohei Ohtani, Will Smith, Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell are all on the wrong side of 30; Tucker will join that list next season. Los Angeles will endure more and more diminishing returns.
That said, nothing (besides a strict salary cap) can really stop the Dodgers from compensating for declining stars by signing more expensive stars, even if it leaves the cap sheet in utter chaos five years from now. That has been L.A.'s strategy to date; it was part of the logic behind the Skubal trade. The Dodgers still arguably represent Skubal's best chance to win a World Series, which will no doubt be part of the calculus if another team can't dramatically outspend them.
1. New York Mets
If any team can blow L.A.'s offer out of the water, it's the Mets. Steve Cohen is baseball's richest owner and New York has consistently tossed its hat in the ring for MLB's premium free agents. Juan Soto's $765 million contract set a new record; Skubal very well could set a record for pitchers.
The Mets are coming off of a last-place season, too, which only fuels anxiety in the fan base. It should also fuel aggression in the front office. David Stearns is under pressure to prove that he has what it takes to win in New York. Skubal would join an emerging ace in Nolan McLean, plus other whippersnappers like Zac Thornton and Jonah Tong. The Mets need depth besides, as Kodai Senga and Sean Manaea look more like bullpen arms these days. New York, however, is the one non-Dodgers team with enough money to sign Skubal and pursue other targets.
If the Dodgers get spooked by the shadow of their own payroll, which is more likely than ever, the Mets are the logical team we can expect to swoop in and win the Skubal bidding war outright.

item.title: [fansided.com] The stars are aligning for the Mets to sign Tarik Skubal, with one giant asterisk standing in their way
item.dc:creator: Zachary Rotman
item.description: The offseason is a perfect time for New York Mets fans like myself to be optimistic, and that's exactly what I'm going to be doing here when I say the stars are aligning for the Mets to sign Tarik Skubal in free agency. I know, this seems crazy. Why would Skubal want to join a Mets team that just won 74 games in 2026 and has failed to make the playoffs in each of Juan Soto's two years in Flushing? Well, here's a look at why the Mets make more sense for Skubal than you might think, and what might
item.content:encoded:
The offseason is a perfect time for New York Mets fans like myself to be optimistic, and that's exactly what I'm going to be doing here when I say the stars are aligning for the Mets to sign Tarik Skubal in free agency. I know, this seems crazy. Why would Skubal want to join a Mets team that just won 74 games in 2026 and has failed to make the playoffs in each of Juan Soto's two years in Flushing?
Well, here's a look at why the Mets make more sense for Skubal than you might think, and what might stand in their way of making this dream of arguably the best pitcher in the sport playing out the rest of his prime in Queens a reality.
The Dodgers' lack of aggression might play into the Mets' hands
When the Los Angeles Dodgers traded for Tarik Skubal, MLB fans not only assumed they'd automatically win a World Series title, but they also assumed that the Dodgers would easily extend Skubal, given their recent history of spending on star-level talent. It's absolutely possible that the Dodgers do choose to re-sign Skubal, but look at what ESPN's Alden Gonzalez had to say about that.
"Skubal's agent, Scott Boras, will probably want to get something done with his client before the lockout, but it would be really difficult for the Dodgers to justify signing Skubal to a massive deal before knowing what MLB's economic model will look like," Gonzalez wrote. "If there is a cap-and-floor system in the next collective bargaining agreement, there will be some sort of phase-in period. But it will undoubtedly impact the Dodgers in the near future. It would be a major risk to sign Skubal before knowing what they're signing up for."
To sum up, Gonzalez is predicting that Skubal's agent, Scott Boras, will likely want to get a deal done with his top client before the expected lockout at the beginning of December, but the Dodgers would want to wait until after the lockout so they know what the economic model of the sport will look like. This makes a ton of sense, given the massive amount of money they've already committed to 2027 and beyond. It's worth noting that this is just Gonzalez's belief, and not a sourced report.
If the Dodgers won't aggressively pursue Skubal before December 1, why can't the Mets be the team to give him an offer he can't refuse? It's not like the Mets haven't been in this position before.
The Mets have beaten the competition to the punch pre-lockout before
Just like a lockout is looming this offseason, one loomed back in the 2021 offseason, when Max Scherzer was a free agent. Scherzer, who was represented by Scott Boras, made it clear that he wanted to sign before the league locked the players out, and he did just that, coming to terms on a three-year, $130 milllion deal with, guess who, the New York Mets.
Now, say what you want about how the deal aged (Scherzer pitched brilliantly in 2022 but struggled in that year's postseason and was traded at the 2023 trade deadline), but the Mets beat the Dodgers and a couple of other teams to the punch to sign the future Hall of Famer on a deal that paid him well over $40 million annually.
Can't that history repeat itself? The Mets won the Scherzer sweepstakes not because they were some powerhouse, but because the Dodgers didn't want to go above and beyond to sign him as the Mets did. Reports suggest Skubal would like to sign pre-lockout and the Dodgers don't want to go above and beyond. Why can't the Mets do what they've already done and give their fan base something to get excited about before the lockout?
If the Dodgers and Mets won't pay Tarik Skubal, what team will?
Let's just assume that both the Dodgers and the Mets decide that paying Skubal is not in their best interest. Is there another team out there willing to spend the $300-to-$400 million on Skubal that he'll likely be asking for?
The New York Yankees are often willing spenders, but with a ton of money invested in starting pitchers like Gerrit Cole, Max Fried and Carlos Rodon, would they pay Skubal before addressing their offense? The Philadelphia Phillies should be eager to spend after another early elimination, but again, is paying on pitching in their best interest? The Chicago Cubs could certainly use the pitching, but they've never even handed out a $200 million contract. Would they give $300+ million to Skubal? The Toronto Blue Jays have the money and the need for pitching help, but they also just paid Dylan Cease handsomely last winter and finished last in runs scored this past season. A return to the Detroit Tigers would be awesome, but that feels unrealistic.
There're other teams like the San Francisco Giants and the Los Angeles Angels who might show interest, but again, there isn't really a perfect fit. If the Mets and Dodgers won't meet an outlandish asking price, which team will?
The Mets have a clear need for a high-end starting pitcher
The Mets are building a strong rotation, with youngsters like Nolan McLean, Christian Scott and Zac Thornton in the fold, but the team lacks a true ace. They hoped Freddy Peralta would fill that void when they acquired him from the Brewers in the 2025 offseason, but that experiment flopped spectacularly.
It's hard to see Skubal flopping, though, at least in 2027. He remains one of, if not the best pitcher in the sport, and even after an early-season injury scare, Skubal ended his season with a 2.72 ERA in 26 starts. He's as dynamic as they come, and would instantly make the Mets true postseason contenders.
If they don't sign Skubal, who else could they realistically get? The next-best options, such as Michael King, Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes, aren't exactly aces. They could potentially swing a trade, but doing so is easier said than done. It feels like Skubal or bust when it comes to getting a bona fide ace.
Would David Stearns be willing to abandon his starting pitching philosophy to sign Tarik Skubal?
We know that the Mets have the need, the money and the location necessary to lure Skubal to the team, but would the individual responsible for making such a move, David Stearns, be willing to do so? Stearns has famously been averse to handing massive deals to starting pitchers, passing on guys like Corbin Burnes, Max Fried and Dylan Cease, to name a few, and instead relying on shorter-term gambles.
Most of these have not paid off, which is partially why the Mets have missed the playoffs in back-to-back years, but will there be a mindset shift? Will Stearns suddenly go from a guy unwilling to offer more than three years to a pitcher over the age of 30 to willing to meet Skubal's demands?
That's an answer we're soon going to learn the answer to, and it could be the difference in Skubal joining the Mets or signing elsewhere. If Stearns is all in, the stars feel like they're aligning for something special to happen.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Red Sox should finally capitalize as insider confirms Padres-Jarren Duran trade interest
item.dc:creator: Katie Manganelli
item.description: After two seasons that ended in the same Wild Card elimination by the same team in the same stadium, upgrading the offense should be the Boston Red Sox's No. 1 priority. item.content:encoded:
After two seasons that ended in the same Wild Card elimination by the same team in the same stadium, upgrading the offense should be the Boston Red Sox's No. 1 priority. There's so much depth in their lineup that there isn't an exceedingly obvious place to add, but it's long been established that their outfield group needs to be shrunk.
Following a career-worst season during which he was one of the worst qualified hitters in the league, trading Jarren Duran seems like an easy answer. Finding a suitor for him after a severe offensive regression and multiple instances of off-the-field drama won't be easy, however.
But MLB insider Jon Heyman reports there's still interest in Duran from one team — the one we all expect. Heyman said in his Bleacher Report live stream that the San Diego Padres are still interested in the outfielder.
The Friars have long expressed their desire to trade for Duran. They've publicly been the team most interested in dealing for him, though there could be others behind the scenes. San Diego once offered Boston Dylan Cease, top catching prospect Ethan Salas and one other prospect for Duran, which the Red Sox "quickly rejected," according to Sean McAdam of MassLive.
MLB insider Jon Heyman says Padres are still interested in Jarren Duran trade with Red Sox
Cease would've just been a rental, but the Red Sox should've taken that deal. They could've extended Cease, but Duran's value was never going to increase — time is ticking down on his contract and he had never shown that he could maintain the level of offensive production he had in 2024, when he earned the All-Star Game MVP and came in eighth in American League MVP voting.
The Padres are likely to lose outfielders Miguel Andujar, Austin Hays and Ramón Laureano to the free agent market, meaning they could use another body in their pastures. Duran's .207/.266/.361 slash line and 165 strikeouts over 151 games are hardly encouraging, but he's a prime change-of-scenery candidate and he could rebound elsewhere.
Boston must prioritize trading Duran (and Masataka Yoshida) not only to give it lineup flexibility, but to open its designated hitter spot for a power bat rather than maintaining the rotating DH structure that it's gone with in recent years. The Red Sox need their top hitters in the lineup every day, and signing or trading for someone who could swap between DH and left field with Roman Anthony is seemingly the easiest way to add power to the lineup.
Trading Duran is also the optimal outcome this offseason because he's regressed so severely that he could be a non-tender risk. At least trading him to the Padres would net the Red Sox a return, however small.
The Red Sox need to clear their outfield logjam if they're serious about improving their offense. Trading Duran should be the first step to their upswing.

item.title: [roundtable.io] Boston Red Sox Starter Nominated for Players’ Choice Award
item.dc:creator: Zach Coe
item.description: Sonny Gray impressed in his first, and maybe only, season in Boston. When the Boston Red Sox acquired Sonny Gray in an offseason deal with the St. Louis Cardinals, they were met with plenty of skepticism about whether or not the 36-year-old veteran could pitch in a big market like Boston after struggling during his time in New York as a member of the Yankees, and whether he could recapture his front-of-the-rotation form this late in his career. item.content:encoded:
Sonny Gray impressed in his first, and maybe only, season in Boston.
When the Boston Red Sox acquired Sonny Gray in an offseason deal with the St. Louis Cardinals, they were met with plenty of skepticism about whether or not the 36-year-old veteran could pitch in a big market like Boston after struggling during his time in New York as a member of the Yankees, and whether he could recapture his front-of-the-rotation form this late in his career. Those two questions he answered emphatically, posting one of the best seasons of his career.
In 29 starts for Boston, Gray posted a 2.72 ERA, the fifth-lowest among qualified American League starters and the eighth-lowest among qualified starters in baseball. In addition to posting the second-lowest ERA of his career, Gray finished the season tied for the league lead in wins with 18. Gray’s career renaissance was especially important in 2026, as the Red Sox lost 2025 American League Cy Young Award runner-up Garrett Crochet to a left shoulder injury on April 26, which ended his regular season. In Crochet’s absence, Gray and rookie Payton Tolle helped carry the Red Sox pitching staff to the third-lowest team ERA in baseball.
As a result of his career renaissance season, Gray has earned a nod of respect from his peers, being named one of the three finalists for the American League’s Most Outstanding Pitcher at the MLB Players’ Choice Awards. Gray is joined by New York Yankees starter Cam Schlittler and Toronto Blue Jays ace Dylan Cease. No surprises among the trio named finalists, as they could very well be the same three named finalists for the American League Cy Young Award.
After putting his name on the map with a dominant Game 3 performance against the Red Sox in the 2025 Wild Card series, Schlittler’s second act was somehow better than his postseason performance. In 33 starts for New York, the Walpole, Mass. native posted a 1.95 ERA, the lowest among all qualified American League starters and second-lowest among all qualified starters in the sport. His spectacular sophomore season is likely to earn him the AL Cy Young Award.
Cease posted an almost equally impressive first season in Toronto. In 29 starts, the 30-year-old right-hander posted a 2.40 ERA, trailing only Schlittler in the American League, and the fourth-lowest mark among all qualified starters in the sport. Cease also continued his run as one of the most prolific strikeout pitchers in the sport, punching out 12.73 batters per nine innings, leading the American League and trailing only Milwaukee Brewers ace and likely National League Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski for the league lead.
The MLB Players' Choice Award winners will be announced during the week of Oct. 26.
Of note
With the Red Sox officially in offseason mode, Zach Coe and David Azer are back on the 'Entering Kenmore' Podcast discussing how close Boston is to winning a World Series, offseason needs, and whether or not the 2026 season was successful. Check it out wherever you get your podcasts, or in the YouTube player below:

item.content:encoded:
An Outstanding first year as a Blue Jay 👨🏻 Dylan Cease is a Finalist for the @MLBPA’s Outstanding Pitcher Award!
Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease nominated for MLBPA’s outstanding pitcher award
Photo credit: John E. Sokolowski-Imagn Images
Dylan Cease’s 2026 greatness has been recognized among his peers. 
On Wednesday, Cease was recognized as one of three American League finalists for outstanding pitcher in Major League Baseball Players Association’s Players Choice Awards. Cease was nominated alongside New York Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler and Boston Red Sox right-hander Sonny Gray. 
Signed by the Toronto Blue Jays to a seven-year, $210-million contract on December 2, 2025, Cease did nothing but impress in his first season north of the border. Cease made 29 starts and went 11-6 with a 2.40 ERA and a 1.10 WHIP. 
Cease struck out 239 batters – tied for third-most with Schlittler in Major League Baseball – and held opponents to a sparkling .180 average. The only pitcher in the majors who beat Cease’s mark of .180 was Milwaukee Brewers right-hander Jacob Misiorowski, who held opponents to a .157 average. 
The 30-year-old’s best month of the season came during July, when the right-hander made five starts and went 3-1 with a 1.00 ERA and 0.72 WHIP. Cease threw 36 innings and, during that span, struck out 46 batters and held opponents to a .125 average. 
Cease spent the month flirting with no-hitters, as on July 8, during a 10-0 win over the San Francisco Giants, the right-hander was three outs away from history before outfielder Heliot Ramos opened the bottom of the ninth with a leadoff single. 
Two starts later, on July 25, Cease turned in a pitching line of 9.0 IP, 1 H, 0 R, 0 ER, 3 BB, 12 K during a 6-0 win over the Boston Red Sox. Cease threw 120 pitches in the outing, in what could be one of MLB’s best pitching performances of the 2026 campaign. 
Unfortunately for Cease, he appeared to run out of gas in September. Following a start against the Texas Rangers on September 18, in which Cease allowed four runs (one earned) across 2.2 innings, it was announced he would head for imaging on his right shoulder. Five days later, Cease was placed on the 15-day injured list, ultimately ending his season. 
With no structural damage, Cease is expected to enter spring training healthy as he prepares for his second season with the Blue Jays.

item.title: [NBC Sports] 2026 Fantasy baseball league winners: Jacob Misiorowski, Jordan Walker, Miguel Vargas, more
item.dc:creator: Eric Samulski
item.description: We’ve had some time for the dust to settle on the 2026 fantasy baseball season, which means it’s time to look back on what we learned (or should have learned) before we turn the page to 2027. I figured I’d start by looking at “league winners.” We love to throw the term “league winner” around, but what does it really mean? I could have looked at all the teams who won leagues and found the players who appeared on most of them. That would be valid, but I don’t have all that data at my fingertips, a
item.content:encoded:
We’ve had some time for the dust to settle on the 2026 fantasy baseball season, which means it’s time to look back on what we learned (or should have learned) before we turn the page to 2027. I figured I’d start by looking at “league winners.”
We love to throw the term “league winner” around, but what does it really mean? I could have looked at all the teams who won leagues and found the players who appeared on most of them. That would be valid, but I don’t have all that data at my fingertips, and I believe the players who “won” you something were the players who outproduced their acquisition cost by the most. So that’s what I looked at: which players produced the most fantasy value based on what it cost to get them. Which players gave you the biggest return on investment. Chances are, if you hit on one or more of these guys, you were in for a pretty solid season.
To measure what their return on investment was, I took the FanGraphs Player Rater dollar values for 12-team leagues and used the Player Rater’s ADP, which is derived from NFBC formats. I compared what each player earned with what his draft position should have earned. The “should have earned” part, I needed some help with, so I had Claude average the 2026 earnings of every player drafted within a reasonable range (about 22%) of the ADP for that pick. So, for example, if the player was the 100th pick, I looked at the value produced by players drafted 78th through 128th. That felt like a fair way to say, “this pick should have produced a value around this amount.”
I referred to that below as their “Slot Cost.” Every pick after pick 250, I also treated as a waiver wire add, which meant it cost nothing to acquire the player. By taking the final dollar value for each player and subtracting their slot cost, we’re left with the players who earned far more than it cost to draft/acquire them.
So who were those players in 2026?
2026 Fantasy Baseball League-Winning Hitters
| Player | Pos | 2026 ADP | Slot cost | 2026 $ | Profit vs slot |
| Pete Crow-Armstrong | OF | 33 | $14.1 | $49.5 | +$35.5 |
| Jordan Walker | OF | 512 | $0.0 | $29.4 | +$29.4 |
| Ben Rice | C/1B/DH | 53 | $9.7 | $36.6 | +$26.9 |
| Miguel Vargas | 1B/3B | 303 | $0.0 | $26.5 | +$26.5 |
| Otto Lopez | 2B/SS | 229 | $0.0 | $26.5 | +$26.5 |
| CJ Abrams | SS | 65 | $9.1 | $33.9 | +$24.8 |
| Sal Stewart | 1B/3B | 162 | $3.3 | $27.9 | +$24.6 |
| Jake McCarthy | OF | 507 | $0.0 | $24.4 | +$24.4 |
| Gabriel Moreno | C/DH | 181 | $0.4 | $24.2 | +$23.8 |
| Alec Burleson | 1B/OF/DH | 175 | $0.9 | $23.9 | +$23.0 |
Not a ton of surprises here. Even though Pete Crow-Armstrong was a top 40 pick, he still vastly outperformed his draft slot. His production so far has exceeded everyone else’s, so he was the ultimate “league winner.” Ben Rice and CJ Abrams were also early-round picks who returned far more than it cost to acquire them, keeping in mind that Rice is catcher-eligible and this is for two-catcher formats.
PCA, Rice, and Abrams also join a group of hitters here who were already pretty good in 2025. Alec Burleson, Miguel Vargas, and Otto Lopez all had flashed usable production in 2025 and were locked into full-time roles. We may not have seen this jump coming, but we likely could have been drafting them higher based on underlying skills and roles.
We have talked ad nauseuam about Jordan Walker‘s breakout and ways in which we could have seen it coming. Sal Stewart was a highly touted rookie who delivered in his first full season, while both Gabriel Moreno and Jake McCarthy earned far more playing time than they were projected to. Moreno had never had more than 380 plate appearances in a season, but had 550 this year, and McCarthy won a starting job in Colorado, which also made him our staff vote for comeback player of the year.
Some other waiver wire players (ADP after pick 250) who came close to making this list were: Dillon Dingler ($22 value in 2026), Liam Hicks ($22), Jake Bauers ($20.8), Carter Jensen ($18.8), Luis Garcia Jr. ($18.6), Kevin McGonigle ($17.8), Carson Benge ($17.8), and Brooks Lee ($14.1).
2026 Fantasy Baseball League-Winning Pitchers
| Player | Pos | 2026 ADP | Slot cost | 2026 $ | Profit vs slot |
| Jacob Misiorowski | SP | 114 | $6.3 | $41.7 | +$35.4 |
| Cam Schlittler | SP | 117 | $5.2 | $37.6 | +$32.4 |
| Drew Rasmussen | SP | 132 | $4.9 | $28.9 | +$24.0 |
| Parker Messick | SP | 294 | $0.0 | $23.0 | +$23.0 |
| Jacob Latz | SP/RP | 731 | $0.0 | $17.6 | +$17.6 |
| Logan Henderson | SP | 413 | $0.0 | $17.4 | +$17.4 |
| Cade Cavalli | SP | 305 | $0.0 | $16.5 | +$16.5 |
| Nick Martinez | SP | 738 | $0.0 | $16.4 | +$16.4 |
| Dylan Cease | SP | 75 | $7.9 | $23.6 | +$15.7 |
| Yoshinobu Yamamoto | SP | 27 | $15.2 | $30.7 | +$15.6 |
Again, we start the list with names that are not particularly surprising. Jacob Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler were the best two pitchers in the league this season, and neither one of them was drafted inside the top 100 picks. Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Dylan Cease were the only two other semi-highly drafted pitchers who produced a “league-winning” return on your investment. I guess we can include Drew Rasmussen in there too.
Of this group of ten pitchers, five of them (Misiorowski, Schlittler, Logan Henderson, Parker Messick, and Cade Cavalli) were high strikeout rate arms who didn’t pitch enough innings in 2025 to be among the top arms drafted. In fairness to drafters, Parker Messick wasn’t officially in the rotation until the end of May, and Cade Cavalli was fairly mediocre until a pitch mix change and velocity bump in the middle of June. Still, betting on strikeout arms coming off limited workload makes sense.
The majority of the other names on here had a clear role/situation change. Drew Rasmussen was another year removed from injury and went up over 170 innings. Nick Martinez was given a chance to be a full-time starter, Jacob Latz was turned into a closer, and Dylan Cease changed organizations, which led to massive improvement from his changeup and attack plan.
So who could fit this bill in 2027?
Potential League-Winning Hitters in 2027
| Player | Pos | 2026 age | 2026 PA | Barrel % | 2026 $ |
| Heriberto Hernández | OF/DH | 26 | 505 | 12.7 | $4.1 |
| Spencer Torkelson | 1B | 26 | 612 | 12.2 | $6.0 |
| Colson Montgomery | 3B/SS | 24 | 638 | 12 | $7.6 |
| Munetaka Murakami | 1B | 26 | 553 | 20.5 | $9.1 |
| Chase DeLauter | OF/DH | 24 | 559 | 6.3 | $10.5 |
| Jac Caglianone | 1B/OF | 23 | 553 | 13 | $14.2 |
| Riley Greene | OF/DH | 25 | 592 | 14.8 | $14.6 |
| Garrett Mitchell | OF | 27 | 531 | 11.7 | $8.3 |
| Wilyer Abreu | OF | 27 | 681 | 12.5 | $13.2 |
| Luis García Jr. | 1B/2B | 26 | 543 | 12.2 | $18.6 |
If we’re going to identify who were league winners in 2026, then it makes sense to use that information to project who would be a league winner in 2027. The hitters who made the league winner list seemed to fall into two categories: Players who had already shown flashes of success and were underpriced (Rice, Burleson, Vargas, PCA, Lopez) and players who experienced a significant bump in playing time from the previous season (Walker, Stewart, McCarthy, Moreno).
It’s hard to use 2026 numbers to project who will have a playing time boost in 2027, so I’ll leave that part to the side for now. To find potentially underpriced hitters, I wanted to look at the commonalities behind the hitters who were “league winners” this year. Among all qualified hitters, having a 12%+ barrel rate or a 91+ mph average exit velocity, combined with being age 26 or younger, doubled the rate of $10+ profits returned. Meanwhile, strikeout rate, walk rate, chase rate, and swinging-strike rate had no relationship to profit.
That means, if we’re looking for players to break out in 2027, we should be looking for players entering their athletic prime who hit the ball hard. Not a shocking revelation, and I already write an off-season column about hitters entering their athletic prime years. This year, that column mentioned Rice, Vargas, Lopez, Ryan Jeffers, Wilyer Abreu, Alejandro Kirk, and a collection of hitters who did not break out (Brett Baty, Heliot Ramos, Andrew Vaughn, etc.)
In addition to the list above, there are a few players who fit the hard contact and age profile but will likely already be priced up by the market. I’m not going to list them as potential league winners, but they should be targets for you in drafts, even at cost: Walker, Stewart, Vargas, Drake Baldwin, Hunter Goodman, Carter Jensen, James Wood and Jackson Chourio. All earned $18–30 this season and could see a sizeable boost from that in 2027.
Of the others listed, Jac Caglianone might be the best fit based on age and his 13% barrel rate and 93.3 mph average exit velocity. We already know why Riley Greene is an exciting fantasy option, but he produced just $15 of value in 2026. There’s a path for him to be a $30+ guy. Heriberto Hernandez and Chase DeLauter could take big steps forward with more playing time; Luis Garcia Jr. has a full season in Yankee Stadium, and all of Spencer Torkelson, Munetaka Murakami, and Colson Montgomery have the batted ball quality but major contact issues. If they can make strides in their contact rates, their power could lead to a massive return on investment for fantasy.
Potential League-Winning Pitchers in 2027
| Player | Team | Pos | 2026 IP | K/IP | 2026 $ |
| Didier Fuentes | ATL | SP/RP | 73.1 | 1.26 | $9.1 |
| Jonah Tong | NYM | SP | 30.2 | 1.13 | -$3.6 |
| Tatsuya Imai | HOU | SP | 76.2 | 1.27 | -$7.3 |
| Gage Jump | ATH | SP | 98.2 | 1.10 | -$15.4 |
| Brandon Sproat | MIL | SP | 97.0 | 1.04 | -$16.3 |
| Jack Leiter | TEX | SP | 80.0 | 1.04 | -$12.8 |
| Jackson Jobe | DET | SP | 46.0 | 1.11 | -$2.1 |
| Mason Montgomery | PIT | SP/RP | 68.2 | 1.54 | $13.3 |
| Grant Taylor | CHW | SP/RP | 84.0 | 1.26 | $13.8 |
Looking at the starting pitchers who made our “league-winners” list earlier in the article, the key is strikeouts. Among all starters drafted at an ADP between 90–400, those who threw under 100 innings in 2025 and posted a 1.0 K/IP or higher averaged $4.40 or more when compared to their slot, and 31% of them returned $10+ profit. So we need to be looking for starting pitchers like that. The names that came up were Didier Fuentes, Jonah Tong, and Logan Henderson. Of course, Henderson already was a “league-winner” in 2026, so his price will be high.
Younger pitchers who had the strikeouts but a poor ERA also fit the bill. Remember that Misiorowski had a 4.36 ERA in 2025. He was missing tons of bats, but the surface-level ratios weren’t ideal. Pitchers like Tatsuya Imai, Brandon Sproat, Jackson Jobe, and Jack Leiter all fit the bill. So did Gage Jump and Mason Barnett, but factoring in the element of pitching in Sacramento muddies those waters.
The other names on this list, Mason Montgomery and Grant Taylor, are either elite closers or potentially breakout starters if they’re moved back into the rotation. There is obviously a lot of uncertainty with their roles in 2027, but they are names to keep an eye on, especially if we have a better idea of their role.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Cubs Won't Get Into ‘Bidding War’ For Seiya Suzuki
item.dc:creator: Joey Pollizze
item.description: It didn't take long for free agent rumors to start swirling. The Chicago Cubs were just swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Round a few days ago, and free-agent rumors are already circling the baseball world. It will no doubt be a busy offseason for the Cubs, who have plenty of players hitting free agency. item.content:encoded:
It didn't take long for free agent rumors to start swirling.
The Chicago Cubs were just swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Round a few days ago, and free-agent rumors are already circling the baseball world.
It will no doubt be a busy offseason for the Cubs, who have plenty of players hitting free agency. Players like Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, David Peterson, and Carson Kelly will all test the open market this winter.
However, the biggest question mark this offseason for the Cubs is what they plan to do with their outfield. Both Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki are free agents at the conclusion of this year's World Series. That leaves the team in a potential rough spot.
The Cubs have to answer one of these questions ahead of free agency:
- Do we bring back both Happ and Suzuki and simply run it back with the same outfield core?
- Do we pay Happ and let Suzuki walk, since he will cost much less?
- Do we pay Suzuki big money and let Happ walk because Suzuki gives us the best chance to win?
The front office will obviously weigh all these options ahead of free agency. However, it seems as if the Cubs have already made somewhat of a decision about Suzuki's future with the organization.
Patrick Mooney of The Athletic reported that "it's unlikely that the Cubs will get into a bidding war for Suzuki's services, let alone win one."
Hearing that the Cubs won't enter a bidding war for Suzuki doesn't bode well for their chances of getting him back. Teams like the Dodgers, Blue Jays, and Yankees are better suited to get into a bidding war for the slugger than the North Siders.
Mitch Bannon of the Athletic already reported that the Blue Jays will pursue Suzuki this offseason. Given that Toronto isn't afraid to spend on big-time players (e.g., Dylan Cease last offseason), there's a strong chance that the outfielder doesn't re-sign with the Cubs.
Losing Suzuki in free agency would be a big loss for the North Siders. He has been one of the team's best power hitters since the Cubs signed him out of Japan in 2022. The Japanese slugger has 113 home runs over his five MLB seasons and has 58 home runs with 189 RBI combined over the past two years.
The Cubs would be losing that power bat at the top of their lineup if he goes to another team. Unfortunately, it's very possible he does leave.

The San Diego Padres blitzed the Chicago Cubs in Game 1 of the NL Wild Card series, 8-0, to put themselves one win away from a date with the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLDS. Plenty of Padres deserve credit for Tuesday night's dominant performance, but none more than soon-to-be-free agent Michael King.
San Diego's ace put together one of the best postseason starts in recent memory, carrying a no-hitter into the seventh inning. He finished with seven scoreless frames, allowing one hit, three walks and recording eight strikeouts. As Padres fans celebrate King's masterclass, prospective free agency suitors are chomping at the bit. Here are a few potential landing spots:
Atlanta Braves
The Braves rotation is a bit scarce behind Chris Sale. Tyler Mahle has eviscerated the competition since arriving at the trade deadline, but he's a free agent next winter. AJ Smith-Shawver, J.R. Ritchie and Owen Murphy are all exciting young arms, but it's unclear which of them will click as full-time starters — and how soon. Martín Pérez, one of this season's great surprises for Atlanta, is also an upcoming free agent.
Atlanta doesn't typically pay sticker price on free agent pitchers but there is immense pressure to compete now — right now — in the twilight years of Sale's career. He won't be able to anchor this rotation forever and the Braves need to start hedging their bets, just in case Father Time catches up.
King, with a 3.21 ERA and 1.18 WHIP, has made 32 starts and pitched a career-high 185 innings this season. The Braves need depth and dependability most desperately, and that's something King can provide. It doesn't hurt that he is building a nice postseason résumé for himself.
Baltimore Orioles
Every winter, we all wonder if Baltimore might finally upgrade its pitching staff. The Corbin Burnes era burned bright and fast. Shane Baz was a savvy trade addition last winter, but the Orioles still struggled to field five quality, healthy starters for the 162-game duration of the regular season.
Trevor Rogers, their best pitcher two years running, will now enter free agency. That leaves Baltimore's front office will a clear and immediate need in the rotation. It seems like the O's new ownership group will, on some level, spend more than the previous administration. The Pete Alonso signing was a stark departure from business as usual in Baltimore. As such, it's not hard to envision the O's ponying up for a second-tier ace like Michael King; the Tarik Skubals of the world are still outside their price range, no doubt.
If Kyle Bradish can finally get healthy for a year, and if the O's deign to re-sign Rogers (or pursue another mid-rotation arm in addition to King), this rotation could shape up quite nicely. Baltimore has the offensive firepower to compete in the AL East. King can help round out a postseason-caliber roster.
Toronto Blue Jays
A nightmare Blue Jays season has finally come to an end, but Toronto should be right back in the postseason fray next season with better luck and an productive winter. The Jays front office is probably the most aggressive in baseball outside of L.A. or New York.
Last offseason, their big fish was Dylan Cease, who immediately turned in a Cy Young-caliber campaign. At the trade deadline, Toronto did not strictly sell, despite sitting near the bottom of the standings. The Jays went out and added José Soriano, another frontline starter at the peak of his powers.
Toronto can expect a healtheir Trey Yesavage in 2027, too, so a premium free agent addition (like King) could quickly transform the Blue Jays rotation into one of the deepest and most fearsome in the American League. If Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and Toronto's boppers put their best foot forward, there's no reason Toronto can't win the division and compete (again) for a World Series.
Houston Astros
The Astros went bullpen against bullpen in their AL Wild Card series opener against the White Sox. Houston was lucky Chicago only managed six runs, with many, many base-runners stranded in scoring position. That did not mean much for the Astros, unfortunately, as the Chicago bullpen — against all odds — mostly kept a more seasoned Houston lineup in check.
Houston has a proper 1A ace in Hunter Brown, but the rotation behind him is total patchwork. Peter Lambert put together a solid campaign and Ethan Pecko faired well in his first taste of MLB action, but the Astros can't really trust anyone besides Brown. Tatsuya Imai, their prized free agent addition last winter, was little more than a bulk reliever in his rookie season.
The Astros have gotten cheaper and cheaper in recent years and the results are getting worse and worse, predictably. Still, this core has competed for a World Series in the not-so-distant past, and we know ownership is capable of spending at the upper echelon of free agency. King would do a lot to solidify the Astros' pitching plans in 2027.
Chicago Cubs
Injuries decimated the Cubs rotation this season. Justin Steele, Cade Horton and Ben Brown should all return in 2027, which is a major, natural influx of talent. If Edward Cabrera can rebound, the Cubs rotation will be all rainbows and sunshine — at least on paper.
But as this season once again reminded us, what happens "on paper" almost never translates to reality. Shōta Imanaga and Matthew Boyd are both upcoming free agents. Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes, Chicago's emergency deadline rentals, are also halfway out the door. There's uncertainty around how exactly the likes of Steele and Horton will perform coming off of major elbow surgeries, too. So the Cubs should play it safe and hyper-focus on pitching depth.
The rotation could be what sends Chicago home against San Diego. So, why not use the Padres own weapons against them in free agency and sign King? "Stability" is a word that comes to mind with King, and that's exactly what the Cubs need right now.
